channel.description: Recent content in Productivity on Best of AI

item.title: Ansible
item.description:
Playbooks describe the desired state of a machine, and Ansible connects over SSH to apply it. It needs no agent on targets. Roles and a large collection of modules cover most common tasks.

The core is free, and Red Hat sells a platform with a controller and support.

Puppet, Chef, and Terraform serve other needs. Ansible suits sysadmins who manage fleets of servers.

item.title: Apache Airflow
item.description:
Workflows are Python files that define tasks and dependencies. A web interface shows runs, logs, and failures. Hosted versions exist from cloud providers and Astronomer.

Airflow handles orchestration, not the data processing itself. It takes effort to run well at scale.

Prefect and Dagster are newer alternatives. Airflow suits data engineers who orchestrate batch pipelines.

item.title: ArborGold
item.description:
Arborists can build quotes from price lists, schedule crews, and send invoices from the field. Mobile apps let crews see jobs and update status. Customer history helps with repeat work and follow-ups.

It is aimed at small and mid-size companies. Features are practical rather than AI heavy.

Jobber and Housecall Pro are broader field service alternatives. ArborGold suits tree care businesses.

item.title: Dagster
item.description:
Developers define assets in Python and Dagster tracks lineage and freshness. A UI shows runs and dependencies, and tests run locally. Dagster Cloud offers a hosted service.

The open-source core is free. It differs from Airflow in structure, so teams moving over need to adjust.

Airflow and Prefect are alternatives. Dagster suits data engineers who want asset-based pipelines.

item.title: Duotrope
item.description:
Writers search by genre, length, pay rate, and reading period. They log each submission and see response times from other users. Listings include submission guidelines and acceptance statistics.

It is a paid subscription with a trial. Statistics come from user reports, so they are estimates.

Submittable and Chills are related tools. Duotrope suits poets who submit work widely.

item.title: Final Draft
item.description:
It handles scene headings, dialogue, and page counts automatically. Writers can use outlining tools, revisions, and collaboration features. Scripts export to PDF and common production formats.

It is a paid program, and its AI features are limited. Some writers prefer Fade In or Highland.

Fade In and WriterDuet are alternatives. Final Draft suits filmmakers and writers who need standard format.

item.title: Floranext
item.description:
Designers take phone and web orders, print tickets, and schedule deliveries. Customer records track occasions for reminders. Online stores are built into the system.

It is a subscription product for flower shops.

Lightspeed and Shopify can work with extra setup. Floranext suits floral designers who run a shop.

item.title: Fresha
item.description:
Salons manage calendars, take payments, and send reminders. Clients find and book services on a marketplace. Reports track sales and staff performance.

The software is free to start, with fees on payments and some features.

Vagaro and StyleSeat are alternatives. Fresha suits cosmetologists and salon owners.

item.title: Jellyfish
item.description:
Leaders see how engineering time splits between roadmap work, support, and tech debt, and track delivery. Resource planning and AI impact reports show effects of tools such as coding assistants.

It is an enterprise product with custom pricing.

LinearB and Swarmia are alternatives. Jellyfish suits engineering managers and executives.

item.title: LinearB
item.description:
Engineering managers see where work waits, such as in review, and set rules to route pull requests. AI features summarize changes and speed up code review.

Pricing is per developer, with a free tier for small teams. Metrics should be used to support teams, not to rank individuals.

Swarmia and Jellyfish are alternatives. LinearB suits engineering managers.

item.title: MassageBook
item.description:
Clients book and fill out intake forms online. Therapists record notes after each session and send reminders. A free plan covers basics, and paid plans add marketing tools.

It is built for solo practitioners and small clinics.

Vagaro and Jane are alternatives. MassageBook suits massage therapists.

item.title: Mindbody
item.description:
Studios set up classes, accept bookings, and manage memberships. Clients book through a branded app or the Mindbody marketplace. Reporting and marketing tools support growth, and AI features help with messaging.

It is a subscription product with tiered pricing.

Vagaro and Zen Planner are alternatives. Mindbody suits yoga instructors who run a studio.

item.title: MoeGo
item.description:
Groomers see appointments by staff and van, store pet profiles, and send reminders. Customers book online and pay by card. AI answers calls and messages in some plans.

It is a subscription product.

Gingr and Pawfinity are alternatives. MoeGo suits pet groomers and small pet service shops.

item.title: Overleaf
item.description:
Several authors can edit the same document, and it compiles to PDF live. Templates cover many journals and conferences. Paid plans add track changes, comments, and version history, and an AI assistant helps with writing and error explanation.

It removes the need to install LaTeX locally. Many universities offer institutional access.

Local LaTeX with a text editor is the alternative. Overleaf suits scientists, mathematicians, and engineers.

item.title: Passare
item.description:
Directors build arrangements, collect e-signatures, and share planning details with families. Obituary and tribute tools help families write remembrances. Reports track revenue and pre-need contracts.

It is a subscription product for funeral homes.

FrontRunner and Osiris are alternatives. Passare suits funeral directors.

item.title: Propared
item.description:
Stage managers build cue sheets, share call times, and send updates to crew. Calendars sync to phones. Documents and rider details stay with each event.

Free and paid plans exist.

Airtable and Notion are general alternatives. Propared suits stage managers and production teams.

item.title: Shopmonkey
item.description:
Technicians and service advisors build estimates from labor guides and parts catalogs, send them to customers for approval, and track the job through completion. Digital vehicle inspections with photos help explain recommended work. Text messaging keeps customers informed.

Shops use it to replace paper tickets and spreadsheets. Parts ordering and accounting integrations vary by plan.

Tekmetric and Shop-Ware are close alternatives. Shopmonkey suits independent repair shops.

item.title: StudioBinder
item.description:
Producers build a schedule from a script breakdown and send call sheets to the crew. Shot lists and storyboards help directors plan coverage. A free plan covers basics, and paid plans add team features.

It suits small and mid-size productions more than large studios.

Movie Magic and Celtx are alternatives. StudioBinder suits filmmakers who run their own productions.

item.title: Swarmia
item.description:
Managers see cycle time, review speed, and where effort goes between features and maintenance. Teams set working agreements and get Slack nudges. Surveys capture developer experience.

It is a subscription product.

LinearB and Jellyfish are alternatives. Swarmia suits engineering managers who care about team health.

item.title: Tekmetric
item.description:
Service advisors write estimates, send digital inspections with photos, and collect approval and payment by text or email. Reports show car count, average repair order, and technician productivity. Integrations connect to parts suppliers and accounting software.

Shops use the data to see what is working and where jobs stall. It is a subscription product with per-shop pricing.

Shopmonkey and Shop-Ware are alternatives. Tekmetric suits independent shop owners and managers.

item.title: Zen Planner
item.description:
Owners set up class schedules and membership plans, and members check in with an app or kiosk. Automated billing reduces missed payments. Reports show attendance and retention.

It is a subscription product.

Mindbody and Kicksite are alternatives. Zen Planner suits martial arts instructors who run a school.

item.title: Adobe Firefly AI Assistant
item.description: Firefly AI Assistant is Adobe’s attempt to bring an agent into its creative apps. Instead of opening each application and applying tools by hand, you describe an outcome, such as adapting a campaign image into several social formats or preparing a video with captions, and the assistant works out the steps. It then carries them out across the right apps in order. The project began under the name Project Moonlight before launching as Firefly AI Assistant.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.description: AgentCore addresses the infrastructure work of taking an agent from prototype to production. A runtime hosts agents with session isolation so each user’s work is kept separate, and handles scaling. Identity features let agents authenticate to other services on a user’s behalf, a gateway turns existing APIs and services into tools agents can call, and observability traces what agents do. Developers can use it with frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, and the Strands Agents SDK, and with models on Bedrock or from other providers.

item.title: Amazon Textract
item.description: Textract turns images of documents into structured data. A developer sends a scanned file or PDF, and the service returns the text it finds along with its layout: it identifies tables and preserves their rows and columns, detects key-value pairs in forms such as a name field and its value, and recognizes handwriting. This is much more useful than plain text recognition, which would return an unordered block of characters.

item.title: AppFlowy
item.description:
AppFlowy is positioned as an open-source alternative to Notion. It offers documents, kanban boards, grids, calendars, and linked databases in a single workspace, and the clients are built with Flutter and Rust for desktop and mobile. You can use the cloud service or host your own server, so notes can stay on hardware you control.

Privacy and ownership are the main selling points. Data is stored locally first, the code is open for review, and teams can modify it. The AI assistant can summarize, rewrite, and answer questions about your pages, and it supports local models through tools like Ollama for people who do not want content leaving their machine.

item.title: Azure AI Document Intelligence
item.description: Azure AI Document Intelligence reads documents so applications can use the data. Its layout model finds text, tables, headings, and selection marks, and prebuilt models recognize common document types such as invoices, receipts, business cards, identity documents, and many tax and mortgage forms, returning fields like totals, dates, and names with confidence scores. You can train custom models with a small number of examples to extract the fields in your own forms.

item.title: Bardeen
item.description:
Bardeen automates repetitive work that happens on web pages. A user installs the extension, then runs playbooks that click through sites, extract data, and send it elsewhere. Typical uses include scraping lists of people from LinkedIn into Google Sheets, saving a company’s details to a CRM, or sending a meeting summary to Slack.

A natural language builder lets users describe what they want, and the AI assembles the steps, which can be edited. Triggers run automations on a schedule or when something happens, and integrations cover hundreds of apps. Sales and recruiting teams, who spend time moving data between tabs, are heavy users.

item.title: Basecamp
item.description:
Basecamp takes a different approach from most project tools. Each project is a self-contained workspace with sections for to-dos, a message board for announcements and discussions, a shared schedule, documents and files, and a group chat called Campfire. Instead of dozens of views and customization options, it offers a fixed, simple structure that’s easy to learn, and encourages asynchronous communication over constant meetings.

The company that makes it, 37signals, is outspoken about its philosophy: calm, focused work and fewer meetings. Features like automatic check-ins replace status meetings, Hill Charts show progress visually, and notifications are designed to be quiet by default. Clients can be invited into projects, which makes it popular with agencies and small businesses.

item.title: Boomi
item.description:
Boomi was one of the first cloud integration platforms. Its visual builder lets teams connect applications and move data between them, with a large catalog of connectors, API management, data integration, and workflow automation in one platform. Companies use it to sync records between sales, finance, HR, and operations systems without extensive custom code.

The company has leaned into AI agents. Boomi lets teams build agents that use connected systems as tools, and offers an agent catalog and controls to track what agents are allowed to do, which matters as companies deploy many of them. Data management and master data tools help keep records consistent across systems.

item.title: Box AI
item.description:
Box is a content management platform, and Box AI brings intelligence to the files stored there. Users can ask questions about a document, compare several files, summarize a long report, or generate text based on content in a folder. The answers come from the files themselves, so they can be traced back to a source.

For businesses, a strong feature is structured data extraction. Box AI can pull fields from invoices, contracts, and forms, such as dates, parties, and amounts, and put them in metadata that others can search and filter. Box AI Agents can be configured for particular workflows, and the platform lets admins choose among models from various providers.

item.title: Claude Cowork
item.description: Cowork takes the agent approach behind Claude Code and puts it in an ordinary app window. Instead of typing commands, you describe a job such as sorting a folder of receipts, turning notes into a report, or building a spreadsheet from several PDFs. Claude breaks the request into steps, makes a plan, works on the files you have shared with it, and reports back when it finishes. Files it reads or creates appear in a panel so you can open them.

item.title: Constant Contact
item.description:
Constant Contact has been a staple of small business email marketing for a long time. Users build mailing lists, design emails from templates with a drag-and-drop editor, schedule campaigns, and track opens and clicks. It emphasizes ease of use and customer support, including phone and chat help, which appeals to owners who are not marketing specialists.

The product extends beyond email. Tools include SMS marketing, social media posting, landing pages, online surveys, and event registration, with automation for welcome series and follow-ups. AI features generate email copy and subject lines, suggest content ideas, and help build campaigns from a short brief, and an AI-driven website builder is part of the suite.

item.title: Databricks Agent Bricks
item.description: Agent Bricks is aimed at companies that want agents grounded in their own data. Rather than writing everything by hand, a team describes the task, such as answering questions over internal documents, extracting information from forms, or coordinating several agents, and the platform helps build it. It generates synthetic test data, evaluates quality with judges, and tunes the agent by trying different models and settings to improve accuracy and cost.

item.title: Dropbox Sign
item.description:
Dropbox Sign lets people sign documents without printing them. You upload a file, mark where each signer needs to sign or fill in fields, and send it by email. Signers open it on any device, sign, and the finished copy is stored with an audit trail that shows who signed and when. Templates make repeat documents such as contracts and NDAs quick to send.

The product started as HelloSign and was acquired by Dropbox, which renamed it. It connects with Dropbox storage, Google Drive, Gmail, Microsoft tools, and CRM systems, so documents can be sent from where they already live. A developer API lets software companies embed signing flows inside their own products, and Dropbox has added AI features in its wider document tools.

item.title: Figma Weave
item.description: Weave brings generative image workflows into Figma. Instead of exporting an image to another tool, a designer can run a prebuilt workflow on a selected layer, for example swapping the background of a product shot, applying an artistic style to an image, or creating variations. More than twenty such workflows cover common creative tasks, and the results land back in the design file, ready to be used in a layout.

item.title: Gemini CLI
item.description: Gemini CLI brings Gemini into the terminal as a coding and automation agent. In a project directory, you describe a task in plain language, such as explaining a codebase, fixing a failing test, or building a feature, and the agent reads files, proposes changes, runs shell commands, and iterates. It can search the web, use a context file to learn project conventions, and work with long contexts thanks to Gemini’s large context window.

item.title: Gemini Code Assist
item.description:
Gemini Code Assist brings Google’s models into the developer’s editor. In VS Code and JetBrains IDEs, it suggests code as you type, answers questions in chat, explains and refactors code, generates tests, and helps fix errors. It can take a larger task and make coordinated changes across files in agent mode. Google also offers a command-line version, Gemini CLI, which many developers use directly in the terminal.

For organizations, enterprise editions add code customization, which lets the assistant take into account a company’s private repositories so its suggestions follow internal libraries and styles, as well as security and compliance features, indemnification, and admin controls. It works with Google Cloud tools such as Cloud Shell, Firebase, and BigQuery, and it can review pull requests on GitHub through a companion app.

item.title: Gemini Spark
item.description:
Spark is Google’s move toward an always-on assistant. You give it jobs, such as pulling together information from your inbox and documents, preparing for a trip, or following up on a task over several days, and it works in the background on dedicated virtual machines in Google’s cloud. Because it runs there, it keeps going even when your phone or laptop is off, and it reports back with results.

Control is part of the design. Spark asks for permission before taking significant actions such as sending messages or making purchases, and users can set skills and schedules to automate recurring work. It starts with Gmail, Docs, and other Google services, and connects to outside tools through the Model Context Protocol and integrations. On Android, a running agent’s progress is meant to be visible at the top of the screen.

item.title: GitHub Agent HQ
item.description: Agent HQ is GitHub’s way of treating coding agents as a team you manage instead of a single assistant. Rather than choosing one AI vendor, a developer can assign work to agents from different providers, such as OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code, from the same place where code, issues, and pull requests already live. Each agent works on its task and returns changes for review in the usual pull request flow.

item.title: GitLab Duo
item.description:
GitLab Duo integrates AI into the places where developers already work in GitLab. In the editor, it suggests code and generates tests, in merge requests it summarizes changes and helps with code review, and a chat assistant answers questions about code, issues, and GitLab itself. For DevSecOps, it can explain security vulnerabilities and propose fixes, and help find the root cause when a CI/CD pipeline fails.

The company has also introduced agent capabilities that can take on tasks across the software lifecycle, such as planning, coding, and review, with human oversight. Because it works within GitLab, it has access to context from repositories, issues, and pipelines, which general assistants lack. Self-managed customers can use it with their own deployment, and organizations control which models and features are available.

item.title: Google Document AI
item.description:
Document AI turns paper and PDF documents into structured data. Prebuilt processors read common document types: invoices with their line items, expense receipts, bank statements, government IDs, and forms. An OCR processor extracts text with layout information, and a layout parser prepares documents for use with language models by splitting them into meaningful chunks.

Customization is a strength. A custom extractor, based on Google’s Gemini models, can be set up with a few examples to pull specific fields from a company’s own documents, even if they vary in layout. A workbench lets teams train and evaluate processors, and a human-in-the-loop option sends uncertain results to reviewers. The output integrates with BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and workflow tools, which helps feed data to analytics and AI systems.

item.title: Graphite
item.description:
Graphite is built around a workflow in which large changes are split into small, dependent pull requests. This stacked approach, popular at big tech companies, lets engineers keep working on the next piece without waiting for the previous one to be reviewed and merged. Graphite provides a command line tool and a web interface that make managing stacks simple, which plain GitHub handles awkwardly.

It adds features around review. A merge queue keeps the main branch healthy by testing and merging changes in order, an inbox helps reviewers see what needs attention, and insights show how long reviews take. An AI reviewer comments on pull requests to catch bugs and style problems, which matters as more code is written by AI assistants.

item.title: Greptile
item.description:
Greptile is an AI code reviewer with a focus on codebase context. Instead of reading only the diff, it builds an understanding of the whole repository, including how functions and modules relate, so comments can point to impacts in files the pull request did not touch.

It posts review comments and summaries on GitHub and GitLab pull requests. Teams can set rules in plain language, and the system learns from thumbs up and down on its comments to reduce noise. An API allows developers to ask questions about the codebase.

item.title: HoneyBook
item.description:
HoneyBook is designed for people who sell services, such as photographers, designers, coaches, and consultants. A client inquiry arrives through a form, the owner sends a proposal with a contract and an invoice, and the client signs and pays online, all within a single flow. This replaces a patchwork of documents, email threads, and payment apps.

Other features support day-to-day work. Automations send reminders and follow-ups, a scheduler lets clients book meetings, and a client portal keeps messages, files, and payments in one timeline. Templates for proposals and questionnaires make repeat work faster, and AI helps draft emails and project descriptions. Reports show income and pipeline.

item.title: Housecall Pro
item.description:
Housecall Pro helps small service companies run their operations. Office staff schedule jobs and dispatch technicians on a calendar and map, customers receive confirmations and arrival notifications, and technicians use a mobile app to see their jobs, send estimates, collect signatures, and take payments on site. Invoices and payments flow into accounting.

The platform includes marketing and sales tools. Review requests, email campaigns, and a customer database help a business grow repeat work, and a booking widget lets homeowners schedule online. Some AI features answer calls and messages, help with scheduling and follow-ups, and summarize job details so owners can stay on top of the business.

item.title: IBM Bob
item.description:
Bob is IBM’s agentic assistant for software development. Instead of only autocompleting code, it takes part in the full lifecycle: understanding a codebase, planning changes, writing and reviewing code, generating tests, and helping with deployment. Different agents take on roles, such as architect or reviewer, and work inside the developer’s editor.

Enterprise use is the focus. IBM emphasizes security and governance, with protection against sensitive data leaks, policy enforcement, and testing of the AI for vulnerabilities. It routes tasks among several language models, including IBM’s own Granite family and models from other providers, and is positioned for modernization work such as moving older Java or COBOL applications.

item.title: Mentimeter
item.description:
Mentimeter makes presentations interactive. You build slides with questions such as multiple choice polls, word clouds, rating scales, rankings, and open-ended questions, share a join code or QR code, and the audience responds from their phones. Results appear live on the screen, which turns a one-way talk into a conversation and gives quiet participants an easy way to contribute.

It suits a range of settings. Teachers use it to check understanding, trainers to energize workshops, and companies to run all-hands meetings and collect anonymous feedback. Features include quizzes with leaderboards, Q&A with upvoting, and templates, and you can import existing slides from PowerPoint or Google Slides. AI helps generate a presentation from a prompt, suggest questions, and summarize responses.

item.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot
item.description: Microsoft 365 Copilot is the business version of Microsoft’s AI, and its main advantage is context. It can see your files, emails, calendar, chats, and meetings through Microsoft Graph, within the permissions you already have. In Word it drafts and rewrites documents based on other files, in Outlook it summarizes long threads and drafts replies, and in Teams it recaps meetings, lists decisions, and answers questions about what was discussed. PowerPoint can build a deck from a document, and Excel can explain formulas and analyze data with plain-language prompts.

item.title: Mistral Vibe
item.description:
Vibe is Mistral’s agent for software work. The command-line version runs in a project directory, reads and writes files, searches code, runs shell commands, and tracks tasks, using Mistral’s coding models to carry out requests such as fixing bugs, adding features, and explaining code. It is open source under the Apache 2.0 license, written in Python, and integrates with editors such as Zed and with other tools.

The broader Vibe offering extends agent capabilities to office tasks and teams. It builds on Mistral’s Devstral coding models and its large general models, which are available through Mistral’s API and, for some, as open weights that organizations can run on their own servers. This flexibility is a selling point for companies and governments that want agents without relying on US cloud providers.

item.title: Morgen
item.description:
Morgen is a calendar and planner. Users connect Google, Outlook, iCloud, and other calendars to see everything in one view, and bring in tasks from tools like Notion, Todoist, and Linear. Tasks can be dragged onto the calendar to block time for them.

The planner feature suggests where tasks fit in the day, taking events, deadlines, and durations into account, and rearranges when plans change. Scheduling links let others book time, with rules for availability and buffers. Frames let users reserve time for certain types of work.

item.title: MURAL
item.description:
MURAL gives distributed teams a shared canvas. Participants add sticky notes, diagrams, images, and text to a large board at the same time, and facilitators run sessions with tools such as timers, private mode for individual thinking, voting, and guided agendas. A big library of templates covers retros, roadmaps, design sprints, and strategy exercises.

AI assists with the messy part of workshops, which is making sense of dozens of notes. It can group sticky notes by theme, summarize a board, and generate ideas to get a session started. Integrations with Microsoft Teams, Zoom, Jira, and Slack connect boards to the tools where work gets done.

item.title: NemoClaw
item.description:
OpenClaw is an open-source agent project that can carry out tasks on a user’s computer and accounts, which made it popular and also raised security worries. NemoClaw is NVIDIA’s response for organizations: it installs OpenClaw inside an isolated runtime, called OpenShell, with strict default permissions, so the agent can only touch what administrators allow. A privacy router helps decide which requests can use outside models and which stay local.

NVIDIA pairs the platform with its Nemotron models and with its NeMo software for building and managing agents, but says NemoClaw works on different hardware and with other models. It was announced with a group of enterprise partners and early integrations with agent frameworks, positioning NVIDIA to offer software as well as chips for the agent era.

item.title: Notion Custom Agents
item.description: Custom Agents extend Notion AI from something you chat with into something that works on its own. A team sets up an agent with instructions and the content it can access, then chooses what should trigger it: a schedule, a comment on a page, a change to a database, an @mention, or messages in a public Slack channel. The agent then does the job, such as triaging incoming requests, compiling a weekly report, updating a tracker, or answering questions in a channel.

item.title: Perplexity Computer
item.description: Perplexity Computer extends Perplexity from answering questions to doing work. You give it a goal, such as researching a market and building a report, tracking a set of sources, or assembling a presentation, and it plans the job, splits it into parts, and runs them, sometimes in parallel. Different steps are sent to different AI models depending on what they are good at, which is the central idea of the product.

item.title: Prezi
item.description:
Prezi stands out for its zooming interface. Instead of a linear deck, you lay out ideas spatially on a big canvas and the presentation moves among them with motion, which gives viewers a sense of how topics relate and can make a talk feel more dynamic. The approach suits overview-and-detail stories and keeps attention better for some audiences than traditional slides.

The product line has expanded. Prezi Video overlays presentation content next to the speaker on video calls and recordings, Prezi Design creates interactive visual content, and the AI assistant generates presentations from a prompt, rewrites text, and builds structure. Templates, brand kits, and analytics help teams use it for sales, teaching, and training.

item.title: Replit Agent 4
item.description: Replit Agent 4 continues the idea that you can describe software and have an agent build it. In the Replit workspace, you explain what you want, and the agent writes the code, sets up the environment and database, tests the result, and deploys it. You review progress, give feedback in plain language, and ask for changes. Replit says this version is substantially faster than its predecessor, which matters because building an app involves many steps.

item.title: Salesforce Agentforce
item.description: Agentforce lets companies deploy AI agents that work inside Salesforce. An agent might answer customer questions, qualify inbound leads, schedule meetings, or update records, using the company’s own data and rules. Builders define an agent’s role, topics, and the actions it may take, connect it to knowledge and data, and test it before release. A reasoning engine decides how to handle each request, and guardrails limit what the agent may do.

item.title: SAP Joule
item.description:
Joule is the assistant inside SAP’s software. Instead of navigating menus in an ERP, finance, or HR system, users ask questions such as which invoices are overdue or what the status of an order is, and Joule retrieves the answer from live business data. It respects the user’s permissions, so it only shows what that person is allowed to see.

It has grown from a question-and-answer helper into a platform for agents. Prebuilt Joule agents handle tasks like processing invoices or supporting recruiters, and Joule Studio lets customers and partners build their own agents and skills that work across SAP and non-SAP systems. SAP presents this as part of a broader business AI platform that connects data and models.

item.title: SAP Signavio
item.description:
Signavio helps companies understand how their processes really work. Teams model processes in a visual notation so everyone can see the intended steps, owners, and rules, and store them in a shared repository. This makes it easier to document, improve, and standardize work across departments.

Process mining adds evidence. By reading event logs from systems like SAP ERP, it reconstructs what happened in practice, revealing delays, rework, and variants that differ from the designed flow. Analysts can then quantify the impact and decide what to fix. Collaboration and journey modeling tools help teams plan transformations such as moving to a new ERP.

item.title: SavvyCal
item.description:
SavvyCal tries to make scheduling feel less like a chore. Instead of a one-sided grid of available times, the invitee can overlay their own calendar, which helps them see conflicts and pick a time that works for both sides. The host can also mark preferred slots, so the invitee sees which options are ideal.

Other features cover business needs. Teams can use round robin and collective scheduling, polls help find a time for groups, and links can be personalized for different meetings. Integrations connect to calendars, video tools, and CRMs, and payments can be collected for paid sessions. Branding options keep the experience consistent.

item.title: ServiceNow Otto
item.description:
Otto is ServiceNow’s way of unifying its AI products into a single assistant. It combines the conversational search that came from Moveworks, the workflow skills of Now Assist, and an agentic interface on the Now Platform. An employee can ask for help in plain language, and Otto finds an answer or starts the workflow that does the job, such as requesting access or opening an IT ticket.

The point is action across systems. ServiceNow positions it as an assistant that works with the enterprise tools a person already uses, not just answering from a knowledge base. Governance is a major theme: AI Control Tower tracks the agents, logs interactions, and enforces policies, which matters when many agents are acting at once.

item.title: Slackbot
item.description:
Slackbot used to be a simple helper that answered canned questions. It has been rebuilt as an agent that works across a Slack workspace. You can ask it to find a decision made in a channel, summarize a thread, draft a message or a document, schedule a meeting from calendar availability, or pull together information from several conversations, and it answers using content you already have permission to see.

Beyond answering, it can take actions. Slackbot can post, set reminders, update records through connected apps, and delegate longer tasks to agents built with Salesforce’s Agentforce, tying Slack more closely to the rest of Salesforce’s platform. Slack has used models from partners to power it, and the assistant adapts to the user’s context and role within the workspace.

item.title: Squibler
item.description:
Squibler is a writing platform for longer projects. Authors plan a book with outlines and a corkboard, write in a distraction-free editor, and track characters, settings, and plot threads. An AI assistant generates outlines, suggests plot developments, and drafts text on request.

It targets novelists, nonfiction authors, and scriptwriters, with templates for different forms and export to formats ready for self-publishing. Collaboration features let editors comment.

Squibler has a free trial and paid plans. AI-drafted text should be edited heavily, and publishing platforms ask authors to disclose AI-generated content. Alternatives include Scrivener, Sudowrite, Atticus, Novelcrafter, and Google Docs. Squibler suits authors organizing long manuscripts.

item.title: Stripe Agentic Commerce Suite
item.description:
As AI agents begin to shop and pay on behalf of people, merchants and payment systems need a way to handle it. Stripe’s suite helps businesses become discoverable to agents: a merchant uploads a product catalog, chooses which agent platforms to sell through, and Stripe handles discovery, checkout, and payments.

It builds on open protocols. The Agentic Commerce Protocol, developed with OpenAI, defines how an agent and a merchant negotiate a checkout. The Machine Payments Protocol, written with Tempo, lets agents and services coordinate payments in code, including small recurring transactions. Stripe also supports an agent wallet and stablecoin payments over the x402 protocol, and it issues limited-use tokens so an agent can spend within set limits.

item.title: Substack
item.description: Substack makes it simple to start a paid newsletter. A writer creates a publication, writes posts in an editor, and sends them to subscribers by email and on the web. The platform handles hosting, email delivery, and payments, so there is no technical setup. Writers can offer free and paid tiers, and subscribers pay monthly or annually, with Substack taking a percentage of paid subscriptions, in addition to payment processing fees.

item.title: Teachable
item.description:
Teachable is a platform for people who want to sell what they know. A creator uploads video lessons, text, and quizzes, organizes them into a course, sets a price, and publishes it on a branded school site. Students enroll, pay, and track their progress, and the creator gets sales and engagement data.

The platform handles the business side. It processes payments in many currencies, supports subscriptions, bundles, and coupons, and offers tools for affiliate programs and email marketing. Coaching products and downloadable files can be sold alongside courses, and certificates reward completion. AI features help draft course outlines and descriptions.

item.title: Thinkific
item.description:
Thinkific is an online course platform. Creators build courses from video, audio, text, and quizzes, organize them into chapters, and host them on a site with their own branding and domain. Students log in to learn, and the platform tracks completion and issues certificates.

Features extend beyond courses. Memberships and communities keep learners engaged, bundles and subscriptions provide pricing options, and integrations connect with email tools, payment processors, and Zapier. Businesses also use Thinkific to train customers, partners, and employees, and AI tools help generate course outlines and quiz questions.

item.title: Trello
item.description: Trello organizes work on a board. Lists represent stages like To Do, Doing, and Done, and each task is a card that you drag from list to list. Cards can hold descriptions, checklists, due dates, attachments, comments, and assigned members. The simplicity is the point: most people learn it in minutes, which makes it popular for small teams, personal projects, content calendars, and simple workflows like hiring or event planning.

item.title: Twilio ConversationRelay
item.description:
ConversationRelay connects phone calls to AI. When a call arrives on a Twilio number, the service converts the caller’s speech to text in real time and streams it over a WebSocket to the developer’s server. The server sends text back, which Twilio converts into speech, so the caller hears a natural response. This lets teams plug in any large language model and their own business logic.

Twilio manages the hard parts of voice. It handles interruptions when a caller speaks over the agent, supports multiple languages and voice providers, and can transfer the call to a human with the transcript. It also offers a no-code Studio widget for simpler flows, plus compliance support for regulated industries, including options for HIPAA and PCI. A reporting feature gives insight into latency and where agents struggle.

item.title: Webex
item.description:
Webex is one of the older names in video conferencing, and Cisco has kept it competitive by adding hardware, calling, and collaboration tools. Companies use it for meetings, webinars, team messaging, a phone system, and conference room devices, with security and compliance controls that suit regulated industries and government.

The AI Assistant adds help across these pieces. It writes meeting summaries and action items, answers questions about what was discussed, catches up people who join late, and summarizes long message threads. Audio features remove background noise and can isolate a speaker’s voice in a loud room, and real-time translation and captions help international teams. Cisco also sells AI agents for contact centers.

item.title: Wrike
item.description:
Wrike is used by teams that coordinate lots of work. Projects can be viewed as lists, boards, Gantt charts, or calendars, and tasks carry dependencies, owners, due dates, and custom fields. Request forms and approvals let outside teams submit work in a structured way, which helps marketing, creative, and operations groups manage intake.

AI features reduce routine effort. Wrike’s tools can summarize long comment threads, create tasks from text, draft project descriptions, and predict which projects are at risk of missing deadlines. Dashboards show workloads and progress across portfolios, and integrations connect to Slack, Salesforce, Microsoft 365, and Adobe tools. Proofing helps creative teams review assets.

item.title: Zapier MCP
item.description:
Zapier MCP turns Zapier’s app library into tools an AI can use. You create an MCP server, choose the apps and actions you want to allow, such as sending a Slack message, adding a row in Google Sheets, or creating a CRM contact, and connect that server to a compatible client. The assistant can then call those actions during a conversation.

This avoids writing custom integrations. Zapier already handles authentication and the quirks of each app’s API, so connecting an assistant to a new service is a matter of adding an action and authorizing your account. You control the scope, and each call uses your connected account, which helps limit what the AI can touch.

item.title: gstack
item.description:
This repository bundles the following skills:

  • office-hours: Asks pointed questions about a product idea before any code is written.
  • plan-ceo-review: Reviews project scope and reframes the underlying problem.
  • plan-eng-review: Reviews architecture, data flow, and test plans.
  • review: Runs a production-focused code review and applies fixes automatically.
  • qa: Tests the app in a live browser and generates regression tests.
  • ship: Opens a pull request and sets up a test framework if one is missing.
  • design-consultation: Generates a full design system for the project.
  • design-shotgun: Produces several visual mockups to explore design directions.
  • cso: Runs a security audit based on OWASP and STRIDE.
  • document-release: Updates project documentation automatically.

item.title: khazix-skills
item.description:
This repository bundles the following skills:

  • leader: Turns vague ideas into clear, actionable goals an agent can execute independently.
  • storage-analyzer: Scans system disk usage and flags files for safe deletion.
  • aihot: Fetches daily AI news summaries and trends without requiring an API key.
  • neat-freak: Aligns project documentation and CLAUDE.md files and audits rule execution.
  • hv-analysis: Produces long research reports, roughly 10,000 to 30,000 words, analyzing products or companies.
  • khazix-writer: Writes long-form content in the creator’s specific style, tone, and voice.

item.title: obsidian-skills
item.description:
This repository bundles the following skills:

  • obsidian-markdown: Creates and edits Obsidian Flavored Markdown files, including wikilinks and callouts.
  • obsidian-bases: Creates and edits Obsidian Bases files with views, filters, and formulas.
  • json-canvas: Creates and edits JSON Canvas files, including nodes, edges, and groups.
  • obsidian-cli: Interacts with Obsidian vaults through the Obsidian CLI.
  • defuddle: Extracts clean markdown from web pages using the Defuddle tool.

item.title: beacon.sh
item.description:
beacon.sh addresses a limit of coding agents: they start each session knowing little about the project. Beacon watches what the agent does, such as commands that work, mistakes it makes, and conventions it discovers, and stores them as notes the agent can use next time.

It works with popular coding agents and keeps the memory in files and a local store the developer can inspect and edit. Over time, that cuts repeated explanations and failed attempts.

item.title: Cedric
item.description:
Cedric acts as a stand-in for meetings. A user gives it slides, notes, and background documents, and it attends a call, presents, and responds to questions using that material. When it does not know something, it can note the question for follow-up.

The idea appeals to people with a heavy meeting load, such as founders or sales teams running repeated demos. It raises etiquette and trust questions: others in the meeting should know they are talking to an AI agent.

item.title: Herdr
item.description:
Herdr manages the growing pile of agent sessions developers run. Instead of many terminal windows, it presents agents in one tabbed interface and shows whether each is working, finished, or waiting for input, when the agent reports status. It supports any agent that runs in a terminal.

The key design choice is the herdr-core runtime, a small server on your machine that runs the sessions. The app is only a front end, so quitting or updating it does not stop agents. A terminal version of Herdr, the original, still exists as a separate program with its own server.

item.title: Claude Duet
item.description: Duet is built on the idea that an assistant should not wait for you to ask. Each morning it sends a brief on what matters across your connected apps, and it checks those accounts every few hours for new items that need attention. You can hand it tasks, and it works on its own virtual machine with a browser, so your laptop or phone does not need to stay on. It keeps working while you are away and tells you when something is done or needs a decision.

item.title: Celonis
item.description:
Celonis is the best-known process mining platform. Every action in business systems, such as creating an order or approving an invoice, leaves a record with a time stamp. Celonis reads these logs and rebuilds the real process, showing the paths that cases take, where they wait, and how often they deviate from the intended flow.

With that picture, teams find delays, rework, and costly exceptions. The platform quantifies the impact, suggests improvements, and can trigger automated actions or alerts. AI features answer questions about process data and recommend where to focus. Common uses include order-to-cash, procure-to-pay, and supply chain work.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, 2026, a week after Claude Opus 5.5. Anthropic says it generates output more than 30% faster than Claude Sonnet 5 while keeping the same API pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached-input reads at $0.20. The context window stays at 1 million tokens.

item.title: DocumentCloud
item.description:
DocumentCloud is a platform built for newsrooms. Reporters upload documents such as court filings, government reports, and leaked files, and the system makes them searchable through optical character recognition. They can annotate passages, add notes, and publish documents so readers can see the original source behind a story.

For large collections, the tool helps with analysis. Entity extraction finds people, places, and organizations mentioned, and search across projects lets teams collaborate on investigations. Add-ons extend the system with automated tasks, including redaction, translation, and data extraction.

item.title: Jobber
item.description:
Jobber is built for small service companies such as lawn care, cleaning, plumbing, and locksmith businesses. Owners send quotes, schedule jobs on a calendar, dispatch crews, and invoice customers, with a mobile app for the crew to see their route, take notes, and collect payment on site.

Client-facing features help win and keep work. Customers can request services online, approve quotes, pay invoices, and receive reminders and arrival notices, and a client hub keeps their history together. Automations send follow-ups and review requests. An AI assistant drafts messages and helps convert rough notes into a clear quote.

item.title: Kajabi
item.description:
Kajabi is an all-in-one platform for knowledge businesses. A creator builds a site, sells courses, memberships, coaching, and digital downloads, collects payments, runs email campaigns, and hosts a community, all from one dashboard instead of stitching together several tools.

Marketing and automation are built in. Landing pages, funnels, email sequences, and a pipeline for leads let creators sell without extra software. The AI assistant helps write copy, plan courses, and generate emails, and analytics show revenue and engagement. Mobile apps for members are available.

item.title: Noterro
item.description:
Noterro is built for small bodywork and rehab practices. Clients book online and fill in intake forms before arriving, and therapists record sessions with notes. An AI feature turns a few prompts into a structured SOAP note, saving time at the end of each appointment.

Other tools cover everyday needs: scheduling, reminders, payments, packages and memberships, and insurance claims where relevant. Reports track revenue and client retention.

Noterro is paid, with plans per practitioner. It is aimed at solo practitioners and small clinics. Alternatives include Jane, Cliniko, MassageBook, Vagaro, and SimplePractice. Noterro suits manual therapists who want simpler admin.

item.title: Paperpal
item.description:
Paperpal is designed for researchers. It works in a web editor, a Word add-in, and a browser extension, checking grammar, clarity, and tone against academic conventions. Suggestions are tuned to scholarly writing, where general tools may flag correct technical phrasing.

Beyond language editing, it offers help with paraphrasing, summarizing, and reference management, plus a literature search feature that finds papers and answers questions with citations. A journal submission check reviews manuscripts against common requirements before submission.

item.title: Productboard
item.description:
Productboard is a product management platform. Feedback from many sources flows into a central place, where it is linked to features and customers. Product managers see which problems come up most and who is asking, which grounds roadmap decisions in evidence.

AI helps process the volume of input. It groups similar requests, summarizes calls and tickets, and drafts specs and release notes. Prioritization frameworks score ideas against objectives, and roadmaps can be shared with stakeholders at different levels of detail.

item.title: SimplePractice
item.description:
SimplePractice is widely used by solo and small group private practices. Clients book appointments online, complete intake forms in a portal, and join video sessions, while clinicians keep notes, treatment plans, and billing in the same system. Insurance claims can be submitted electronically.

AI features help clinicians write progress notes from session details and speed up documentation, which is a chief burden for therapists. The platform offers reminders, reporting, and a client app for messaging and payments.

item.title: Spectora
item.description:
Spectora is software for home inspection businesses. Inspectors document a property on a phone or tablet, adding photos, notes, and ratings, and Spectora compiles a professional report that can be delivered to clients and agents. Scheduling, agreements, and payment tools run the business side.

AI speeds up the slow part. It helps summarize defects, produce clear language for findings, and organize repair requests, and voice dictation turns spoken notes into text. Reports include summaries that buyers and agents can use during negotiations.

item.title: StyleSeat
item.description:
StyleSeat serves independent beauty professionals. Clients search for stylists, browse portfolios and reviews, and book appointments, while professionals manage their calendar, take deposits, and process payments through the platform.

The marketplace helps new clients find providers, and the business tools handle reminders, no-show protection, and client records. Recommendations use location and preference data to match clients.

StyleSeat has a subscription for professionals and fees on some transactions. Fees for marketplace clients can be a concern for stylists with an existing following. Alternatives include Vagaro, Fresha, Booksy, Square Appointments, and Glossgenius. StyleSeat suits independent stylists and barbers.

item.title: Transkribus
item.description:
Transkribus is built for historical documents. Archivists and researchers upload scans of handwritten or old printed material, and the platform transcribes them with models that can be trained on a specific hand or period. The result is searchable text that can be corrected and exported.

It grew from European research projects and is now run by a cooperative, READ-COOP. Thousands of archives, libraries, and genealogists use it, and public models cover many languages and eras. AI search finds words across collections.

item.title: Trinka
item.description:
Trinka is built for scholarly and professional documents. It reviews text for grammar, style, and consistency with academic conventions, and understands field-specific terms in areas like medicine, engineering, and law. Suggestions explain why a change is recommended.

Extra tools check for plagiarism and consistency, offer paraphrasing, and run publication readiness checks. Plugins work with Microsoft Word and browsers, and a web editor is available.

Trinka has a free tier and paid plans. Authors should follow journal policies on AI-assisted editing. Alternatives include Paperpal, Grammarly, Writefull, Wordvice AI, and QuillBot. Trinka suits researchers and students polishing manuscripts.

item.title: Vagaro
item.description:
Vagaro runs the front desk for beauty and wellness businesses. Clients book online or through a marketplace app, staff manage calendars, take payments, and track inventory. Reminders and no-show protection reduce lost appointments.

Marketing tools include email and text campaigns, loyalty programs, and a presence on the Vagaro marketplace. AI answers calls and messages, helps book appointments, and suggests promotions.

Vagaro charges a monthly fee per business, with add-ons and payment processing fees. Alternatives include Fresha, Booksy, StyleSeat, Square Appointments, and Mindbody. Vagaro suits salons, spas, and studios.

item.title: OpenAI Dots
item.description: Dots move ChatGPT from a tool you open to an assistant that keeps working. Each dot has its own cloud computer with a browser, so it can carry out tasks on websites and in apps without tying up your device. You give it goals, such as keeping track of your inbox, preparing for meetings, or monitoring a project, and it works in the background, checking back when it needs input. Over time it learns from your feedback.

item.title: ByteAsk
item.description:
ByteAsk positions itself around a less glamorous part of software work. Most AI coding tools focus on writing new code, but a large share of an engineer’s time goes into finding why something breaks, why a service is slow, and keeping older systems healthy. A tool focused on that work would read logs, traces, and code to find causes and suggest fixes.

That area is promising because debugging depends on context that general assistants lack, such as how a particular system behaves in production. It also carries risk, since a wrong fix can make things worse, so suggested changes need review and testing before they ship.

item.title: Ando
item.description:
Ando rethinks team chat for a workplace where software agents work next to people. In most chat tools, AI is an add-on bot. In Ando, agents have identities, inboxes, and permissions, and they can join channels, read ongoing conversations, and message teammates, just like human members.

The product has the familiar parts of a messaging platform, including channels, direct messages, group conversations, and calls. The difference is how agents are treated: a person can assign work to an agent in a thread, and the agent can respond, ask questions, and report back. Teams can bring agents built on different models.

item.title: Claude Docs
item.description:
Claude Docs brings document writing into the chat. Instead of copying an answer from a conversation into another app, you ask Claude to draft a report, memo, or plan, and it appears as a document you can edit beside the conversation. You can revise it by typing changes directly or by asking Claude to rework sections.

Documents are stored in the Artifacts tab, so they are easy to find later and update across sessions. When the draft is ready, it can be exported to common formats such as Word, PDF, Google Docs, or Markdown. The tool handles headings, lists, and tables, and it works with files and context shared in the conversation.

item.title: Claude Slides
item.description:
Claude Slides makes decks from a conversation. You describe the audience and the point of the presentation, share notes or source files, and Claude produces a set of slides with an outline, text, and layout. You can then ask for changes, such as a different order, a tighter message, or new visuals, and edit individual slides directly.

The finished deck can be presented from within Claude or exported to PowerPoint or PDF for use elsewhere. Because it lives in the same place as the conversation, you can pull information from uploaded documents and revise based on feedback without switching tools. It sits alongside Claude’s other creation features, including Docs.

item.title: MosMos
item.description:
MosMos is a dictation and meeting tool for Mac. A user speaks and text appears in the active app, formatted to fit the context: casual in a chat, structured in a document, code-friendly in an editor. A personal glossary learns names and technical terms, reducing repeated mistakes.

In meetings, MosMos can record and transcribe with labels for each speaker and produce notes and action items afterward. Combining dictation and meeting features in one app saves switching between tools.

item.title: Google CC
item.description:
CC acts like a morning assistant. Each day it sends an email, called Your Day Ahead, that pulls together calendar events, important messages, bills, and documents relevant to the day. You reply to the email to ask for changes, such as adding an event or digging into a topic, and CC acts on it.

It connects to a user’s Gmail, Calendar, and Drive and can also use the web for context. Because it works through email, there is no new app to learn. Google has expanded the experiment to support shared use by members of a household, with each person connecting their own accounts.

item.title: Meta Muse
item.description: Muse is Meta’s step from a chat assistant to an agent that acts on your behalf. You ask it to do something, such as arrange a trip, draft and send an email, or handle a multi-step errand, and it works across apps and websites to complete the job. Each user’s agent runs in a secure virtual machine, so it can continue working after you leave the app and come back when it needs a decision.

item.title: Almanac
item.description:
Almanac builds memory for an AI agent. Once you connect work accounts, it reads messages, calendar events, documents, and code activity and compiles what it learns into a wiki covering people, projects, and decisions. The wiki updates as new information arrives, so the agent does not start from zero each time.

The agent then uses that knowledge to do work. Teammates can send requests through tools such as Slack, and it checks the wiki for context before acting, which aims to reduce the repeated explaining that other assistants need. Connections can be personal or shared, so a company can decide how much of its information the agent sees.

item.title: Aloud
item.description:
Aloud addresses the gap between what a developer means and what ends up in a written bug report or feature request. It records voice, screen, and a live transcript while someone talks through an app the way they naturally would, pointing at elements and changing their mind mid-sentence. It then converts the recording into a clean set of instructions.

The output is formatted so coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex can act on it directly. The tool flags anything that could be read two ways and attaches relevant screenshots, which cuts down on back-and-forth. Speech transcription runs locally through Whisper, so recordings stay on the Mac and are not uploaded, which matters for work on client or proprietary code.

item.title: Codex
item.description:
Codex works as a software engineering agent. A developer describes a task, such as fixing a bug or adding a feature, and Codex explores the code, makes a plan, edits files, and runs tests or linters to verify the result. It reports back with a summary of what it changed and why.

It comes in several forms. A command line tool runs on the developer’s machine, a desktop app manages multiple tasks, extensions integrate with editors like VS Code, and a cloud version in ChatGPT runs tasks in isolated sandboxes, often in parallel, and can propose pull requests on GitHub. Configuration files let teams give the agent project instructions.

item.title: GitNexus
item.description:
GitNexus gives coding agents a map of a codebase. It analyzes repositories and builds a graph in which nodes are symbols, files, functions, and services, and edges show how they relate, such as which function calls another. Agents query the graph over the Model Context Protocol to answer questions like what will break if this function changes.

The aim is more reliable context than searching text or embeddings, which can miss relationships. The graph can span multiple repositories, which helps in organizations with many services. It works with different agents and editors, and the vendor claims it lowers cost and errors.

item.title: OpenCode
item.description:
OpenCode is a coding agent that works in a developer’s terminal. It reads a repository, plans changes, edits files, and runs commands, with a text interface for conversation. The same engine also runs behind a desktop app, editor extension, and web client.

Provider freedom is the main appeal. Users connect models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others, or open models run locally, and can switch between them. Configuration files add project rules, custom agents, and Model Context Protocol tools, and sessions can be shared.

item.title: Zetik
item.description:
Zetik is a personal research assistant. A user picks topics, and the system monitors many source types, ranks what matters, and delivers a concise brief, so they stay informed without scanning feeds. It aims to surface signal across places that are hard to follow manually.

This suits founders, investors, and researchers who track fast-moving fields. Summaries need to link back to sources, and personalization improves as the tool learns what the user finds relevant.

item.title: Meta Muse Code
item.description:
Muse Code is Meta’s entry into agentic coding. A developer starts it in a project folder, describes a task, and the agent explores the code, plans changes, edits files, and runs tests, working across a repository rather than on single files. It is powered by a Meta model tuned for coding.

Meta presents it as a lower-cost option next to tools from Anthropic and OpenAI, and it runs from the command line on macOS and Linux. Features such as running sub-agents in parallel aim at larger tasks. The tool was released in beta, so expect changes.

item.title: Google Antigravity
item.description:
Antigravity is Google’s take on an AI-first coding environment. Instead of a chat panel beside the editor, agents have direct access to the editor, the terminal, and a browser, so they can write code, run it, test the result in a browser, and report back with artifacts such as plans, screenshots, and recordings that show what they did.

Developers can run several agents in parallel and manage them from a control view. Later versions added background tasks that run on a schedule and a standalone command line tool. The environment uses Google’s Gemini models and can work with other models.

item.title: Kiro
item.description:
Kiro is built around spec-driven development. A developer describes a feature, and Kiro produces a requirements document, a technical design, and a task list. The developer reviews and edits these, and the agent then works through the tasks, writing code and tests. The idea is to keep an agent aligned with intent on larger work instead of improvising from chat.

The editor is based on Code OSS, so VS Code extensions and settings carry over. Hooks trigger agent actions on events such as saving a file, steering files give persistent guidance about a project, and support for the Model Context Protocol connects external tools. It uses Claude models through AWS.

item.title: Elastic AI Assistant
item.description:
Elastic AI Assistant is built into the Elastic stack, which many companies use for search, logs, and security monitoring. Users ask questions in plain language, such as what caused a spike in errors or what an alert means, and the assistant queries the data, explains findings, and suggests next steps.

For security teams, it helps triage alerts, write queries, and summarize incidents using the organization’s own data. For observability, it assists with investigating logs and metrics. Retrieval from indexed content grounds answers in real information, and administrators choose which language model provider to connect.

item.title: Figma Make
item.description:
Figma Make lets designers and product teams bring ideas to working form. A user describes an app, or starts from a Figma design, and the AI builds an interactive version using code. They can then edit it by chatting, adjusting on the canvas, or changing the code directly.

Because it connects to Figma, designs, components, and styles can serve as the starting point, which keeps results consistent with a design system. Teams use it to test ideas with realistic prototypes before involving engineering, and to share working demos with stakeholders. Backend features such as data storage let prototypes behave more like real apps.

item.title: Born to Found
item.description:
Born to Found guides first-time founders through the early journey. It divides company building into stages, such as validating an idea, building a first product, and finding customers, and supplies playbooks and checklists for each, so a founder knows what to focus on at their point.

An AI coach answers questions and reviews work, drawing on the founder’s stage and project details. This offers a low-cost alternative to mentors for people who lack access to experienced advisors, and a structure to keep going when the path is unclear.

item.title: ChatGPT Work
item.description: ChatGPT Work extends ChatGPT from answering questions to doing jobs. You describe an outcome, such as preparing a weekly status report, building a slide deck from a folder of notes, or reconciling figures between two spreadsheets, and the agent works through it step by step. It gathers context from connected tools, uses a browser and code when needed, and produces finished files. Tasks can run for a long time without you watching, and you can return to review the result.

item.title: AICode
item.description:
AICode targets a problem many AI coding tools handle poorly: older systems with hundreds of files and years of accumulated decisions. Where an assistant that autocompletes in a single file struggles, a tool built for legacy code needs to understand how modules depend on each other and what a change will affect.

The pitch includes helping developers navigate unfamiliar code, explain what a function does and why, plan refactors, and write documentation or tests. Teams that inherit a system with little documentation can use that kind of help to get productive faster. Work on large code usually depends on good context retrieval and on careful human review of suggested changes.

item.title: AIPRM
item.description:
AIPRM saves people from writing prompts from scratch. Its browser extension adds a prompt library to the ChatGPT interface, organized by topic such as SEO, sales, customer support, productivity, and writing. You pick a prompt template, fill in details like your topic or audience, and it sends a detailed, well-structured instruction to the AI. Users can also create, save, and share their own prompts.

The library grew from community contributions, which means quality varies, though ratings and usage counts help identify useful ones. Paid plans add private prompts, team sharing, and prompt management for organizations, plus integrations with other AI tools. It is popular with marketers and SEO professionals who run the same kinds of tasks repeatedly, such as keyword clustering or content briefs.

item.title: Bloomfire
item.description:
Bloomfire is a knowledge management platform. Employees add articles, files, videos, and Q&A to a central library, tag them, and find them later with search. The platform is meant to hold what a company knows so that people do not keep asking colleagues the same questions.

AI features make retrieval easier. Users ask questions in plain language and get answers drawn from the company’s own content with links to sources, and the system can suggest related material and flag content that needs updating. Analytics show what people search for and where gaps exist.

item.title: C3.ai
item.description:
C3.ai builds packaged AI applications and a platform for developing them. Instead of starting from scratch, a company can adopt an application for a defined problem, such as predicting when equipment will fail, detecting fraud, or optimizing inventory, and connect it to their data. The platform provides tools for data integration, modeling, and deployment.

The company has moved to add generative AI. Its offerings include tools that let users ask questions about enterprise data in natural language and agent features for business workflows. Customers include utilities, manufacturers, banks, and defense and government agencies, where large-scale deployments are common.

item.title: Cal.com
item.description:
Cal.com is an alternative to Calendly built around openness. Users connect their calendars, define when they are free, and share a link that lets others book a slot. Event types handle one-on-one meetings, group sessions, and team round-robin assignments, and bookings sync to video tools and calendars.

Because the code is open source, companies can self-host it and customize it, or embed scheduling inside their own products with APIs and components. Workflows send reminders and follow-ups, payments can be collected at booking, and routing forms direct prospects to the right person. AI assistants can handle scheduling conversations.

item.title: ConvertKit
item.description:
ConvertKit was designed for independent creators rather than traditional businesses. It makes it easy to build a list with forms and landing pages, tag subscribers by interest, and send newsletters and automated sequences. The company later renamed the product Kit, and the old name remains widely used.

Creator commerce is a major part. Users can sell digital products, paid newsletters, and subscriptions directly, with payments handled in the platform. A recommendation network lets creators promote each other’s newsletters, and automations route subscribers based on what they click. AI tools help draft emails and subject lines.

item.title: GetResponse
item.description:
GetResponse bundles several marketing tools. Users collect subscribers with forms and landing pages, send newsletters, and build automated workflows that respond to behavior such as signing up, clicking, or buying. A webinar feature lets businesses host live events and follow up with attendees.

AI helps create content. An assistant drafts emails, subject lines, and landing pages, and builds campaigns from a short brief, while segmentation and analytics help improve results. E-commerce features include product recommendations and abandoned cart emails, and integrations connect with online stores and CRMs.

item.title: Laxis
item.description:
Laxis joins online meetings, records and transcribes them, and produces summaries with action items and key points. Sales teams use it to log call notes in the CRM automatically, and researchers and recruiters use it for interviews. Search across past meetings helps find specific topics.

Extra features include templates for different meeting types, follow-up email drafts, and analytics on conversations. Integrations connect with Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and CRMs such as Salesforce and HubSpot.

item.title: Mailchimp
item.description:
Mailchimp is one of the best-known email marketing services. You build an audience list, design emails with a drag-and-drop editor or templates, and send campaigns with reporting on opens and clicks. Automations send welcome series, abandoned cart reminders, and birthday messages, and signup forms and landing pages help grow the list. It also supports basic CRM features, social posting, and simple websites.

AI is built into content and targeting. Generative tools help write subject lines and email text, and build designs from a brand’s assets. Predictive segmentation estimates customer behavior, such as likelihood to buy, and send-time optimization chooses delivery times. Intuit’s AI assistant brings help with questions about campaigns. Integrations connect with Shopify, WooCommerce, and hundreds of other apps.

item.title: MailerLite
item.description:
MailerLite offers the core tools of email marketing without clutter. Users build a list, design emails with a drag-and-drop editor, set up automations that respond to subscriber behavior, and publish landing pages and sign-up forms. Websites and simple stores can also be built within the platform.

Features include segmentation, A/B testing, an AI writing assistant, and e-commerce integrations with Shopify and WooCommerce. Analytics show opens, clicks, and revenue. Paid subscription newsletters are supported, which has drawn creators.

item.title: PDF.ai
item.description:
PDF.ai lets people interact with documents. A user uploads a PDF, and an AI answers questions about it, with references to the pages where the answers appear. It can summarize chapters, pull out key points, and extract data.

It is used for papers, contracts, reports, and manuals, where reading everything is time consuming. Page citations let users verify answers, which matters because language models can misread or invent details.

PDF.ai has a free plan with limits and paid tiers. Sensitive documents deserve a check of the privacy policy. Alternatives include ChatPDF, NotebookLM, Humata, Claude and ChatGPT with file uploads, and AnythingLLM for local use. PDF.ai suits people who work with long PDFs.

item.title: Rewatch
item.description:
Rewatch is built on the idea that useful knowledge is trapped in recordings no one rewatches. It captures meetings and async videos, transcribes them, and organizes them into channels and playlists, so employees can find the moment they need by searching words said.

Features include summaries, chapters, comments on moments in the video, and integrations with Zoom, Slack, and calendars. The goal is to let people catch up on meetings quickly and reduce the number of live sessions.

item.title: Warmbox
item.description:
Warmbox addresses a deliverability problem. New or little-used email accounts sending outreach often land in spam. Warmbox connects an account to a network of inboxes that exchange emails, open and reply to them, and gradually build a positive sending history.

It is used before and during cold email campaigns, with dashboards that show inbox placement and health. Settings control volume and ramp-up.

Warmbox is paid, with plans by mailboxes. Warm-up does not fix poor targeting or bad content, and spam laws still apply. Alternatives include Instantly, Smartlead, Lemwarm, Mailreach, and Warmup Inbox. Warmbox suits teams sending cold email.

item.title: Writer
item.description:
Writer targets large organizations that need AI output to stay on brand and compliant. Teams set style guides, terminology, and rules, and the system applies them as people draft, with checks for claims and tone. A knowledge graph lets AI answer from company data.

The company builds its own Palmyra language models and a platform for building agents that handle multi-step work across tools. Governance features such as permissions, logging, and fact checks support regulated industries.

item.title: Bonsai
item.description:
Bonsai bundles the paperwork of independent work. A freelancer sends a proposal, converts it into a contract with e-signature, tracks time or milestones, sends an invoice, and receives payment. A client portal keeps everything in one place, which helps a one-person business look established.

Additional tools cover running the business. Expense tracking, tax estimates, and banking features support finances, and workflow automations send reminders for unpaid invoices. AI helps draft contract language and project descriptions. Templates are available for design, consulting, development, and other fields.

item.title: JITX
item.description:
JITX approaches board design as software. Instead of drawing a schematic by hand, an engineer describes circuits and requirements in code, and the system selects parts, creates connections, and generates a board layout that satisfies rules for signal integrity, power, and manufacturing. Changes can be made by editing the description and regenerating.

That makes it easier to reuse designs, check them automatically, and explore alternatives. The platform’s solvers handle routine layout tasks, so engineers concentrate on architecture. It targets hardware teams that build complex boards and want faster iteration.
