The app shows your total planned hours against the day’s available time, which discourages overcommitting.

It connects to many other tools. Tasks from project managers, issue trackers, email, and Slack can be brought into your daily view without leaving Sunsama, and calendar events appear alongside them. An end-of-day shutdown ritual lets you review what you finished and move unfinished tasks forward. AI features help with suggestions for scheduling, summaries, and organizing tasks.

item.title: Superhuman
item.description:
Superhuman became known as the fastest email client. It’s designed so you can process your inbox with the keyboard, using commands for archiving, replying, snoozing, and reminders, and everything loads instantly. The interface is minimal, with Split Inbox sections that separate important mail from newsletters and notifications. Features such as send later, follow-up reminders, read statuses, and a command palette are built into the workflow.

AI is now part of the experience. It drafts replies in your voice, summarizes long threads, searches your mail in plain language, and can write emails from short prompts. The company that owns Superhuman acquired it, changed its own name to Superhuman, and groups it with Grammarly’s writing assistant and the Coda workspace in a combined suite.

item.title: Supermaven
item.description: Supermaven was a coding assistant that focused on one thing: fast, accurate autocomplete. Its main claim was an unusually large context window, which let it consider much more of your project than most completion tools when suggesting the next lines. Developers liked how quickly suggestions appeared, and extensions for VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and Neovim made it easy to try. A free tier and a low-priced paid plan helped it spread.

item.title: Supernormal
item.description:
Supernormal aims to make meeting notes require no effort. A bot joins your scheduled meetings, records and transcribes them, and creates notes organized by templates for different types of meetings, such as sales calls, interviews, one-on-ones, and standups. The notes list decisions, action items, and key points, and are shared with attendees or saved to the tools your team uses.

The product works across platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, and also supports in-person meetings. Integrations push notes to Slack, Notion, HubSpot, Salesforce, and Google Docs. Search and chat features let you look back at past meetings and ask questions, and customization options allow you to adjust the format of the notes.

item.title: Tactiq
item.description:
Tactiq takes a lightweight approach to meeting notes. Instead of sending a recording bot into the call, it runs as a browser extension that captures the meeting’s captions and audio on your device. A live transcript appears in a sidebar as people speak, and you can highlight key moments as the meeting happens. That makes it less intrusive in calls where an unfamiliar bot would raise eyebrows.

After the meeting, AI features produce summaries, action items, and custom outputs from prompts, such as a follow-up email or a status update. The transcript is saved in your account and can be exported to tools like Notion, Google Docs, Slack, and HubSpot. Templates adapt the output for different meeting types, and a search function finds past conversations.

item.title: Tana
item.description:
Tana combines outlining with databases. Everything is a node in an outline, and tagging a node with a Supertag gives it fields and behavior, so a note about a person, a book, or a project becomes structured and can be queried and viewed in many ways. Backlinks connect related ideas.

AI is integrated into the workflow. It can transcribe meetings and turn them into tagged notes, fill in fields, and answer questions across a workspace, and it can act on commands users define. Voice capture makes it easy to record ideas on the go.

item.title: Taskade
item.description:
Taskade merges project management and AI. A project can be viewed as a list, board, calendar, table, or mind map, and everything can be edited collaboratively in real time. Chat and video calls are built into the workspace so a team can discuss and track tasks in one place. It is flexible enough for personal to-do lists, team projects, wikis, and meeting notes.

AI agents are central. Users can create agents with specific roles and knowledge, such as a research assistant, a project manager, or a support bot, and let them generate content, break down projects, and respond to questions. Automations connect actions across tools and trigger agents on schedules or events, and templates cover common uses like content planning and sales processes. You can also generate whole projects from a prompt.

item.title: Textio
item.description:
Textio focuses on how words affect people at work. Its model, trained on large amounts of text paired with outcomes like application rates, flags language in a job posting that may discourage certain candidates, such as gendered phrases or jargon, and suggests alternatives that attract a broader and larger pool. Recruiters get a score and specific edits as they write.

The platform extends to employee communications. Textio helps managers write clearer, fairer performance reviews and feedback by spotting vague, biased, or unhelpful phrases, and supports recruiting emails and other HR writing. Generative AI features help draft job posts and feedback from a few inputs while applying the same guidance. Integrations work within applicant tracking systems and email tools.

item.title: tl;dv
item.description:
tl;dv, short for “too long; didn’t view,” saves people from rewatching meetings. A bot joins your calls to record and transcribe them in many languages, and you can mark highlights during the call. Afterward, the recording is available with an AI-generated summary and a list of action items, plus timestamps so you can jump to the part that matters. Clips can be shared with people who missed the meeting.

The tool is popular with sales and product teams. It can fill in CRM fields in tools like HubSpot and Salesforce, produce reports across many meetings to spot patterns such as customer objections, and send notes to Slack and Notion. Templates tailor summaries to sales calls, user interviews, and team meetings, and search lets you find topics across your library.

item.title: Toast
item.description:
Toast serves the restaurant industry. Servers take orders on handheld devices, kitchen displays route tickets, guests pay at the table or online, and managers track sales, labor, and inventory. Online ordering, delivery integrations, and loyalty programs are part of the ecosystem.

Data and AI support operations. Sales forecasts help schedule staff, menu analytics show what sells, and assistants help write menu descriptions and answer business questions. Payroll and team management tools extend the suite.

item.title: Todoist
item.description: Todoist is a clean, fast task manager. You add tasks by typing in plain language, like “send report every Friday at 3pm,” and it turns that into a recurring due date. Tasks can be organized into projects and sections, given priorities and labels, and viewed as a list, board, or calendar. Filters let you build views such as everything due today across all projects. It syncs across phones, computers, browsers, and email clients.

item.title: Tome
item.description:
Tome became a popular early example of generative AI for presentations. A user described a topic, and Tome produced a complete, designed narrative with text, images, and layout, which could be edited in a flexible, canvas-like format. It was positioned as a more modern, storytelling-focused alternative to PowerPoint, and gained millions of users, with attention from students, founders, and professionals.

The company later decided to retire the presentation product and pivot to something different, a sales-focused application. Users were given a period to export their work before the service closed. The pivot reflected a challenge facing many AI tools: general features are quickly matched by larger products, and a standalone app needs a defensible niche.

item.title: Tray.io
item.description:
Tray.io builds on the idea of integration-platform-as-a-service. Teams use a visual builder to create workflows that connect SaaS applications, databases, and internal systems, with powerful logic, error handling, and the ability to write code where necessary. Hundreds of connectors and a universal connector for APIs cover common enterprise tools such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack.

The company has moved toward AI agents. Its Merlin AI tools let teams build agents that use the connected systems as tools, so an agent can look up a customer, update a record, and send a message, with governance over what it can access. Embedded integration products let software companies offer customer-facing integrations in their own products.

item.title: UiPath
item.description:
UiPath popularized robotic process automation, in which software robots mimic what a person does on a screen. Developers build automations in a studio by recording and arranging steps such as clicking, copying data between systems, and filling forms, and run them on servers or desktops. This is valuable for companies with legacy systems that lack APIs, since bots can work through the same interfaces people use.

The platform has expanded into AI. Document understanding extracts data from invoices and forms, process mining reveals which workflows are worth automating, and agent tools let AI agents plan and carry out tasks, orchestrated alongside robots and people. The Maestro orchestration layer coordinates agents, robots, and human steps, and governance features control access and auditing.

item.title: Visme AI
item.description:
Visme is aimed at people who need to present information visually without design skills. It offers a drag-and-drop editor with thousands of templates for presentations, infographics, reports, charts, social media posts, and documents. Data widgets create charts and graphs from spreadsheets, and interactive elements such as links and animations can be added. Brand kits keep colors, fonts, and logos consistent across a team.

AI features speed up creation. An AI designer can generate a presentation or document from a prompt, write and rewrite text, create images, and suggest layouts. Teams can collaborate in real time with comments and workflows, and content can be exported as PDF, PowerPoint, or HTML, or shared by link with analytics. Visme is often used by marketers, educators, consultants, and communications teams.

item.title: WordAI
item.description:
WordAI is an article rewriter. You paste in text, and the tool produces a reworded version that keeps the meaning but changes the sentences and structure. It was one of the earlier products built around natural language processing for this job, as opposed to older spinners that swapped in synonyms and produced awkward results.

People use it to adapt copy for different audiences, create alternate product descriptions, or refresh older posts. Settings control how much it changes, and you can review and edit the output. It sits alongside the Spin Rewriter and Chimp Rewriter type tools, and now competes with general AI assistants that can rewrite on request.

item.title: Wordsmith
item.description:
Wordsmith turns data into text. Users define templates and logic, connect a data source, and the platform writes a narrative for each record, such as a financial summary, a sports recap, or a personalized report. The output is consistent and can be produced in volume.

It predates today’s chat models. Rule-based natural language generation gives predictable text, which suits regulated reporting where exact control matters, while large language models offer flexibility and fluency but less predictability.

item.title: Workato
item.description:
Workato is an integration and automation platform. Teams build recipes that link applications such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack, trigger actions, and move data. Business users can create simple automations while IT governs the platform.

The company has added AI across the product. Users describe a workflow in plain language and Workato builds a draft, document understanding extracts data, and agents handle tasks with enterprise controls. Governance, security, and monitoring suit regulated companies.

item.title: Writerly
item.description:
Writerly is aimed at teams that want AI-written content to sound like them. Instead of generating generic text, it lets users supply samples of their existing writing and style guidelines, then drafts articles, emails, and social posts that follow that voice. That approach is common among brand-focused writing tools, and matters most for companies with several writers.

Features reported in directories include templates for common content types, collaboration for editors and reviewers, and options to reuse past content. Teams often use this kind of tool to keep messaging consistent across channels and to speed up first drafts, with humans editing for accuracy and judgment.

item.title: Writesonic
item.description: Writesonic began as a template-driven AI writer for marketing copy. You choose a type of content, such as a blog post, ad, product description, or social caption, fill in some details, and get a draft. A longer-form article writer builds full posts with an outline, headings, and optional SEO guidance, and a chat assistant answers questions and can search the web. A browser extension and integrations with WordPress and other tools help get content published.

item.title: x.ai
item.description: x.ai took a distinctive approach to scheduling. Instead of an app or a booking link, you copied its assistant, Amy or Andrew, on an email thread, and it handled the back-and-forth of finding a time with the other people. It read your calendar, proposed times in natural language, replied to the guests, and sent calendar invitations. Because everything happened by email, the other person did not need to install or log in to anything.

item.title: Zapier
item.description:
Zapier handles the plumbing between business apps. A workflow listens for an event in one tool and does something in another, with filters, paths, and delays to model real processes. Templates cover common needs in sales, marketing, and operations.

Newer capabilities include AI actions that read and write text, agents that carry out multi-step tasks, and an MCP offering that exposes Zapier actions to AI assistants. Teams can monitor runs, handle errors, and manage access centrally.

item.title: Zapier
item.description: Zapier connects the apps a business already uses and lets them pass data to each other without code. You build a Zap with a trigger, such as a new form submission, and one or more actions, such as adding a row to a spreadsheet, posting in Slack, and creating a CRM contact. It supports thousands of apps, from Gmail and Salesforce to niche tools, which is the main reason people choose it over building integrations by hand. Filters, paths, and delays let a Zap branch and wait, and a multi-step workflow can handle surprisingly complicated processes.

item.title: Zed AI
item.description:
Zed is built for speed. Its editor, written in Rust, starts quickly and stays responsive on large projects, and multiplayer editing lets several people work in the same file with voice and chat.

AI is built in rather than added by extension. Users chat with models in an assistant panel, ask for inline edits, and run an agent that edits code across files, with support for several providers and local models. Edit predictions suggest the next change as you type, and the Agent Client Protocol lets other agents run inside.

item.title: Zoho
item.description:
Zoho builds a wide range of business applications on its own platform. Companies can use Zoho CRM for sales, Books for accounting, Desk for support, Projects for work tracking, Mail for email, People for HR, and dozens of other apps, many of which integrate with one another. Zoho One bundles the whole suite for a single per-user price.

Zia is the AI layer. It predicts which leads are likely to convert, detects anomalies in data, drafts replies, and answers questions in natural language, and Zoho has added a generative assistant and agents that can act across apps. The company also supports the option of running models on its own infrastructure for customers who want data kept in their region.

item.title: Notion
item.description: Notion works as a set of building blocks. A team can create a company wiki, a project tracker with a board view, a product roadmap, a meeting notes database, and a documentation site, all in one workspace with permissions and comments. Databases are central: the same set of records can be viewed as a table, board, calendar, or timeline, and linked to other databases, which makes it possible to build custom systems without code.

item.title: ABBYY
item.description:
ABBYY has worked with optical character recognition for decades. Its FineReader software converts scanned pages and PDFs into editable text, and its enterprise products read invoices, contracts, IDs, and forms at scale. Machine learning classifies the type of document, locates key fields such as invoice totals and dates, and extracts the data in a structured form that other systems can use.

The platform has expanded into intelligent document processing. Pre-trained skills handle common document types without training, while companies can build custom models for their own forms. Validation tools route low-confidence results to human review, and integrations connect with robotic process automation, ERP, and content management systems. ABBYY has added generative AI features and tools for making documents ready for use by language models, as companies seek to feed documents into AI workflows.

item.title: Aide
item.description: Aide was an AI-first code editor from the London startup CodeStory. It was a fork of VS Code, so it looked familiar and could use extensions, but it added a layer of AI that understood the project. You could chat about the codebase, ask for changes across several files, and get completions informed by wider context. It was released as open source under the AGPL license, and the project drew substantial interest from developers looking for an alternative to Cursor.

item.title: Alexa AI
item.description:
Alexa popularized the smart speaker. You speak to an Echo device to play music, set timers, control lights, check weather, shop on Amazon, and ask questions. Over the years, it grew into a platform with thousands of skills from third parties and support for a huge range of smart home devices. It’s built into many speakers, TVs, cars, and appliances.

Alexa+ is the next generation. Built on large language models, including Amazon’s own Nova and models from other providers, it holds more natural conversations, understands context across a dialogue, and can handle multi-step requests such as planning an evening, booking a reservation, or coordinating a family calendar. It can act across services, remember preferences, and work with smart home devices more flexibly, and a web and app experience complements the voice interface. Some promised features arrived later than first shown.

item.title: Augment Code
item.description:
Augment Code is built for teams with big, long-lived codebases. Its main idea is deep context: the tool indexes the repository and related documentation, so suggestions reflect the project’s own APIs, conventions, and architecture, not generic patterns. That reduces the made-up function calls common with less informed assistants.

It works in the editor with chat, inline completions, and next-edit suggestions that anticipate where you will change code next. Agent features take on larger tasks such as implementing a feature or fixing a bug across files, with the developer reviewing changes. A command line tool and integrations extend it into other workflows, and enterprise options address security and data handling.

item.title: Beehiiv
item.description:
Beehiiv is built for people who run newsletters as a business. Writers compose and send posts, manage subscriber lists, and publish a website for the archive. Growth tools include referral programs, recommendations between newsletters, and landing pages, which help build an audience without outside ads.

Monetization is a central feature. Creators can sell paid subscriptions, run ads through the Beehiiv ad network, add sponsors, and offer digital products. Analytics show opens, clicks, and which posts convert readers. An AI assistant helps with drafts, subject lines, and ideas, and automation handles welcome sequences.

item.title: Cosine
item.description:
Cosine aims to act like a teammate on a codebase. It indexes the repository, then takes tasks such as fixing a bug or adding a feature, planning the work, editing multiple files, and running tests. It explains its reasoning along the way so a developer can follow and step in.

The company trains its own models, called Genie, specialized for software engineering using data on how developers work. Tools include a command line interface, an editor extension, and a web app, and it integrates with GitHub for pull requests. It also offers deployments for organizations with security needs.

item.title: Docsumo
item.description:
Docsumo turns documents into structured data. A company uploads or emails PDFs and scans such as invoices, receipts, bank statements, and forms, and the platform reads fields and tables, checks them against rules, and sends clean data to accounting, lending, or ERP systems. This replaces manual entry.

A review interface lets staff correct uncertain fields, and corrections improve accuracy over time. Pre-trained models cover common documents, while custom models handle company-specific layouts. Workflows include validation rules, approvals, and integrations through APIs. Lenders and finance teams are major users.

item.title: Document360
item.description:
Document360 helps companies maintain help centers and internal documentation. Writers use an editor with categories, versioning, and review workflows, then publish to a branded site that customers or employees can search. Analytics show what people look for and which articles fall short.

AI makes content easier to find and keep up to date. Semantic search finds answers by meaning, a chatbot answers questions from the documentation, and suggestions point out gaps and outdated articles. Writers can also use AI to draft and improve content. Integrations connect with helpdesk and chat tools.

item.title: Factory AI
item.description:
Factory sells AI agents for engineering teams. Droids take tasks from tickets or chat, explore a codebase, make changes, run tests, and open pull requests for review. Specialized droids handle different jobs, such as code review, incident response, or migrations.

The product works through a command line tool, IDE integrations, and a web interface, and connects to GitHub, Jira, Slack, and other tools so agents fit into existing workflows. Enterprise features address security, permissions, and model choice, with support for several model providers.

item.title: Fantastical
item.description:
Fantastical is known for natural language entry. A user types a phrase such as lunch with Sam next Tuesday at noon, and the app creates the event with the right time, place, and attendees. It shows calendars from many accounts in one view, including Google, iCloud, and Exchange, along with tasks and reminders.

Scheduling features help with coordination. Users can share availability and let others book time, propose several slots to a group, and attach video conference details automatically. Newer AI features help with preparation for meetings and smart suggestions, and the app integrates with other tools through its calendar sets and openings.

item.title: Ghost
item.description:
Ghost is a publishing tool focused on independent media. It provides a clean editor, a website with themes, email newsletters, and a membership system that lets readers subscribe for free or pay. Because it is open source, publishers can host it themselves or use Ghost’s managed service.

Business features are built in. Payments run through Stripe, so publishers keep most of the revenue, and analytics show how posts convert readers into members. The platform supports multiple tiers, comments, and integrations with other tools. A nonprofit organization develops it, which differs from venture-backed rivals.

item.title: Guru
item.description:
Guru stores verified knowledge in cards that teams can find where they work. A browser extension and Slack integration surface relevant answers without leaving the page, and experts verify cards on a schedule so that the information stays trustworthy. The idea is a single source of truth for sales, support, and internal teams.

AI search connects to the company’s other sources, such as documents, chat, and ticketing systems, and answers questions in natural language with citations. Analytics show what people search for and which content is stale. Admins control who can see what, and the AI respects those permissions.

item.title: HyperScience
item.description:
HyperScience automates paperwork-heavy processes. Organizations in insurance, banking, and government feed forms, letters, and claims into the platform, which classifies each document, extracts fields, and passes clean data to downstream systems. Handwriting recognition covers documents that older tools struggled with.

A human-in-the-loop design handles low-confidence results: reviewers check flagged fields, and their corrections improve the models. The platform has added large language model features for understanding unstructured text and answering questions about documents, and it supports on-premises and private cloud deployment for sensitive data.

item.title: HyperWrite
item.description:
HyperWrite started as a writing tool that predicted and completed text as you typed. It grew into a suite that includes a document editor, a browser extension that works across websites, and tools for rewriting, summarizing, and researching. Users can generate text from prompts and refine it in place.

The company has focused on agents. An assistant can navigate web pages, fill in forms, and complete multi-step tasks in the browser on a user’s behalf, which fits its idea of a personal AI assistant. It supports multiple underlying models.

item.title: Instabase
item.description:
Instabase focuses on complex documents that older template-based tools could not handle. Mortgage packages, insurance claims, and financial statements arrive in many formats, and Instabase uses AI models to classify them, extract data, and validate it against rules. Results flow into systems such as loan origination and claims platforms.

Its platform provides tools for building document workflows with a mix of models and human review, and newer products use language models for understanding and answering questions about documents. Customers can deploy it in the cloud or in their own environment, which matters for regulated data.

item.title: Jira
item.description:
Jira tracks work through issues in boards, backlogs, and timelines. Software teams use it for sprints, bug tracking, and roadmaps, and many other teams use it for requests and projects. Workflows are customizable, and it integrates with code hosts, chat tools, and the rest of Atlassian’s products.

Atlassian has added AI across Jira. It summarizes long ticket discussions, drafts descriptions and subtasks, and turns natural language into search queries. Rovo agents can take on work such as triaging issues or answering questions across connected tools, and the AI draws on a team’s own data.

item.title: Nanonets
item.description:
Nanonets turns documents into data. A company sends invoices, purchase orders, receipts, or forms by email or upload, and the platform reads them, extracts fields and line items, and validates them against rules. Approved data flows into accounting or ERP systems.

Pre-trained models cover common documents, and teams can train models for their own layouts with a few samples. Workflows add approval steps, matching against purchase orders, and exception handling. Language models help with messy or varied documents.

item.title: Paragraph AI
item.description:
Paragraph AI brings AI writing to the smartphone. A user types a few words or dictates an idea, and the app produces a full email, message, or post, which can be adjusted for tone, length, or formality. Rewrite and proofreading tools tidy existing text.

The appeal is convenience for writing on the go, when opening a full desktop assistant is awkward. Typical uses include replying to emails, drafting social captions, and polishing short messages.

item.title: PearAI
item.description:
PearAI is a standalone editor forked from VS Code, with AI features built in. Developers get code completion, a chat panel that understands the project, and inline editing, and can connect their preferred models. Because it is a fork, familiar extensions and settings carry over.

It positions itself as an open alternative to Cursor and Windsurf. The AI layer builds on Continue, an open-source assistant. The project had a licensing controversy early on regarding its use of existing code, which it has since addressed.

item.title: Plandex
item.description:
Plandex works in the terminal and aims at tasks that span many files. It plans a change, builds it up in a sandbox so edits can be reviewed before they touch your project, and supports long context windows to keep track of large repositories. Changes can be rolled back, and different models can be used for different steps.

The team behind it announced that Plandex Cloud would wind down, leaving the self-hosted open-source server and CLI. That means new users need to run it themselves, and development activity has slowed, so check the repository for current maintenance.

item.title: Poolside
item.description:
Poolside focuses on one domain: code. The company trains large models from scratch, using reinforcement learning where the model writes code, runs it, and learns from whether it works. The aim is models that handle real software tasks reliably.

It targets customers with strict security needs, such as defense and large enterprises, and offers deployment in their own environments. Products include a coding assistant and an agent built on its models, and the company has invested heavily in computing infrastructure.

item.title: Reducto
item.description:
Reducto turns messy documents into clean data. A developer sends a PDF or image, and the API returns structured output that preserves layout, tables, and figures, which can feed language models or databases. It combines vision models and traditional techniques to handle difficult pages.

Applications include financial analysis, legal review, healthcare records, and RAG systems where poor parsing hurts answer quality. Options exist for extracting fields to a schema and for splitting documents by type. Enterprises can deploy it in their own environment.

item.title: Refact.ai
item.description:
Refact.ai gives developers an assistant they can control. It offers autocomplete, chat that understands the codebase, and an agent that can carry out tasks like fixing bugs, running tests, and refactoring. It plugs into popular editors.

Privacy is a key benefit: companies can run it on their own servers with open models so code never leaves their environment, or use cloud models. Fine-tuning on a codebase is available in some setups.

item.title: Relay
item.description:
Relay.app takes the Zapier-style approach and adds two things: AI steps and humans in the loop. A workflow can trigger on an event, call an AI to summarize or draft, then pause for a teammate to approve before the next action runs. This suits tasks where full automation is risky.

Integrations connect common business tools, and a visual builder makes flows easy to design. Examples include drafting replies for review, routing leads, and preparing reports. Approvals can be done in email or Slack.

item.title: Rossum
item.description:
Rossum reads business documents without fixed templates. Companies receive invoices in many formats, and Rossum identifies fields such as vendor, amount, and line items, validates them against rules, and sends clean data to accounting or ERP systems.

A review interface lets staff correct uncertain fields, and the system learns from corrections. Workflows handle approvals and matching with purchase orders. The company has moved to a transactional language model approach for understanding documents.

item.title: Shortly AI
item.description:
Shortly AI was one of the early GPT-based writing tools built for fiction and long-form content. A writer types, and with a keystroke the assistant continues the text in the same voice, or offers rewrites and alternatives. It aimed to keep the writer in control of the direction.

It was used for blog posts, stories, and essays, particularly to push through slow stretches. The product emerged before general chat assistants became widely used, and those assistants now cover much of the same ground.

item.title: Slab
item.description:
Slab gives teams a clean place to write and organize internal documentation. Content is arranged in topics, and the editor emphasizes readability. Engineering, support, and operations teams use it for runbooks, handbooks, and policies.

Search is the core feature. It queries Slab content and connected tools such as Google Drive, GitHub, and Slack in one place, and the AI answers questions in natural language with links to sources. Verification features prompt owners to keep pages up to date.

item.title: Spike
item.description:
Spike presents email like a chat. Threads become conversations, which can feel faster, and a unified view combines email with notes, tasks, and calendar. Teams can discuss messages privately without forwarding.

AI helps with summaries of long threads, drafting replies, and organizing the inbox, and shared inboxes support small teams. It works with many email providers.

Spike has a free tier and paid plans. Chat-style email is a taste, and some prefer traditional layouts. Alternatives include Superhuman, Shortwave, Hey, Gmail with Gemini, and Front. Spike suits people who want a conversational inbox.

item.title: Sweep AI
item.description:
Sweep started as an AI junior developer on GitHub. A user described a task in an issue, and the bot read the code, planned changes, and opened a pull request. The team found it hard to reach the reliability they wanted and noticed that most AI coding attention was focused on VS Code.

They pivoted to a JetBrains plugin for IntelliJ, PyCharm, and other IDEs, offering context-aware chat, multi-file apply, and automated code review. The plugin can run in on-premises settings, which suits companies with security needs.

item.title: Tettra
item.description:
Tettra helps teams keep answers in one place. Teams write pages for policies, processes, and FAQs, organize them in categories, and assign owners who verify content periodically so it stays accurate. Integrations with Slack make answers available where people ask questions.

An AI assistant searches the wiki and connected sources to respond to questions in chat. Requests that cannot be answered become tasks for subject experts, which grows the knowledge base over time.

item.title: Activepieces
item.description: Activepieces is an alternative to Zapier built with openness in mind. Users build automations called flows by chaining a trigger, such as a new form entry, to actions across apps like Google Sheets, Slack, Gmail, and CRMs. The editor is friendly to non-developers, and code steps are available for custom logic. The integrations, called pieces, are open-source and community-contributed, and each can also work as a tool for AI agents.

item.title: Adobe Acrobat AI
item.description: Acrobat AI Assistant adds a chat panel to the PDF reader most offices already use. Open a contract, report, or research paper, and you can ask for a summary, a list of action items, or an answer to a specific question. Each answer links back to the passage it came from, which makes it practical to check the work instead of trusting it blindly. It handles long files that would take an hour to skim.

item.title: Aider
item.description: Aider is a command-line tool for pair programming with a language model. You start it inside a git repository, add the files you want to work on, and describe what you want in plain English. It edits the files directly, shows the diff, and commits each change with a sensible message, so you can review or undo anything the model did with ordinary git commands. That tight git integration is what makes it feel safe to use on a real project.

item.title: AIWriteBook
item.description:
AIWriteBook is aimed at people who want to produce a book without doing every step by hand. The workflow starts with a topic, generates an outline, drafts chapters, and offers editing passes. Extras include cover design and formatting for publishing platforms such as Amazon KDP.

Tools like this attract self-publishers, especially in nonfiction niches. They also raise concerns. Books produced mostly by AI can lack depth, accuracy, and a personal voice, and readers and platforms are wary of low-effort content. Amazon requires authors to disclose AI-generated content when publishing, and quality problems lead to poor reviews.

item.title: Akiflow
item.description: Akiflow is built for people whose tasks are scattered across many apps. A task might arrive as an email, a Slack message, a Jira ticket, or an Asana item, and Akiflow collects them in a universal inbox so you can decide what to do and when. You drag tasks onto a calendar to block out time for them, which turns a long to-do list into a realistic day. Keyboard shortcuts and a command bar make it fast to use.

item.title: Amazon Q Developer
item.description: Amazon Q Developer is the successor to CodeWhisperer, and it is built around AWS knowledge. In VS Code, JetBrains, and other IDEs it offers inline code suggestions and a chat panel that explains code, writes tests, and optimizes functions. In the terminal, it adds autocomplete and a chat that can translate plain language into shell commands. In the AWS console and on chat platforms like Slack, it helps troubleshoot services and explains why a resource is misbehaving.

item.title: Automateed
item.description:
Automateed focuses on turning an idea into a finished ebook quickly. A user enters a topic or outline, the tool drafts chapters, and the author edits and arranges them. The platform then handles formatting and export in common ebook formats, with covers and other publishing steps in the workflow.

The audience is self-publishers and marketers who produce lead magnets, guides, and short nonfiction books. The convenience comes with tradeoffs. Mostly machine-written books can be generic, may contain factual errors, and face skepticism from readers and retail platforms. Amazon asks authors to disclose AI-generated content when publishing.

item.title: biela.dev
item.description:
Biela.dev belongs to the group of prompt-to-app tools. A user describes the product they want, and the platform generates the code for the interface and logic, previews it in the browser, and lets the user request changes in conversation. When satisfied, they can deploy it online.

These tools suit prototypes, internal utilities, and early product tests. They shorten the path from idea to something clickable, which helps founders show investors or customers what they have in mind. Generated code can be exported for developers to continue.

item.title: Bolt.new
item.description: Bolt.new turns a conversation into a working application. You type what you want, such as a booking site, a dashboard, or a small SaaS prototype, and Bolt writes the code, installs the dependencies, and runs the result in a live preview in your browser. You can keep asking for changes, and it edits the project as you go. It is built on StackBlitz’s browser-based development environment, so nothing needs to be installed on your computer.

item.title: Bookbud
item.description:
BookBud.ai gives authors an AI workspace for book projects. A writer provides a premise or notes, and the tool proposes outlines and drafts sections of chapters, which the author reworks. The idea is to keep momentum when a blank page is the biggest obstacle.

Self-publishing authors use such tools to move faster, but quality depends on the human in charge. AI drafts tend toward the generic and can repeat or contradict themselves over a long manuscript. Readers value distinct voice and accuracy, and retail platforms ask authors to disclose AI-generated content.

item.title: Capacities
item.description: Capacities rethinks how a notes app is structured. Instead of one kind of page, everything you capture is an object with a type, such as a book, a person, a meeting, an article, or a project, and each type can have its own properties and template. You link objects together, so a book can connect to the people who recommended it and the ideas it inspired. The result is a graph of your knowledge that is easier to browse than a pile of untitled notes.

item.title: ChatPDF
item.description: ChatPDF is a simple tool for talking to a document. You upload a PDF or paste a link, and it reads the file and lets you ask for a summary, a definition, or a specific fact. Each answer includes references to the pages it came from, so you can check the passage yourself. Students use it to understand dense papers, professionals use it for contracts and reports, and people use it to find the right section of a long manual without scrolling.

item.title: Choosaro
item.description:
Choosaro structures the way you decide. You list the options, such as three laptops or two job offers, then define the criteria that matter, like price, quality, or location, and assign each a weight. Scoring the options against the criteria produces a ranked result that shows which choice best fits your priorities.

The method is a weighted decision matrix, a familiar technique that makes tradeoffs explicit. Writing criteria down helps people notice what they really care about and gives teams a shared basis for discussion. AI features can suggest criteria and help fill in details.

item.title: Cline
item.description: Cline is an autonomous coding assistant that lives in your editor. You describe a task, and it works through it: reading the relevant files, proposing edits, running commands, and checking the result. It has a Plan mode, where it explores the project and agrees an approach with you, and an Act mode, where it carries the plan out. Each file change and terminal command is shown for your approval, so you stay in control, though you can switch on auto-approval for lower-risk actions.

item.title: Collate
item.description:
Collate focuses on private document work. A user opens a PDF, such as a paper, contract, or textbook, and asks questions about it or requests a summary. Because the processing runs locally on the device, the document does not need to leave the computer, which matters for sensitive files.

Typical uses include studying, reviewing research papers, and pulling key terms from long reports. Local models are smaller than cloud models, so results are good for summaries and questions about the text but may be less strong on complex reasoning, and speed depends on the hardware.

item.title: Continue
item.description:
Continue is built around choice and control. Instead of locking users to one provider, it lets them plug in the model they prefer, from cloud APIs to models running locally with Ollama, and configure how it behaves with rules, prompts, and context from their codebase and documentation.

The extension offers autocomplete, chat that can reference files and docs, and an edit mode that rewrites selected code. Teams can share configurations and use Continue’s hub for sharing assistants, and the project has expanded to automated checks that run on pull requests. Because the code is open, companies can audit and adapt it.

item.title: Denovo
item.description:
Denovo aims to shorten the path from idea to launched business. A user describes what they want to start, and the platform helps produce a business plan, suggests names and branding, generates a website, and walks through setup tasks such as registering the company. Putting these steps in one tool reduces the number of services a beginner must find and learn.

The target is people who have never started a company, or who want to test a side project quickly. AI-generated plans and sites provide a starting point, and users still need to validate demand with real customers and check legal requirements in their location.

item.title: Devin
item.description: Devin is designed to work like a junior engineer who can take a ticket and run with it. It has its own cloud environment with a terminal, code editor, and browser, so it can clone a repository, install dependencies, write code, run tests, look up documentation, and keep trying when something fails. When it is done, it opens a pull request with its changes and a summary. You can interact with it while it works, and you can run several Devin sessions in parallel on separate tasks.

item.title: Fabricate
item.description:
Fabricate belongs to the group of prompt-to-app tools. A user describes the application, and the platform generates the interface, server logic, and data storage, then deploys it so it can be used right away. The user keeps refining by asking for changes in chat.

It is meant for prototypes, internal tools, and simple products. Getting from idea to something usable in minutes helps founders test concepts. Generated applications need testing, and authentication, payments, and security deserve a careful look before launch with real users.

item.title: Hedy AI
item.description:
Hedy AI takes a different role from notetakers that summarize afterward. It listens during a call or conversation and shows prompts in the moment: a suggested answer, a question to ask, or a reminder of context. The goal is to help the user perform better while the conversation is happening.

After the meeting, it produces transcripts and summaries and can store notes for future sessions. People use it for sales calls, interviews, negotiations, and learning situations. It can run alongside video calls or in person on a phone or computer.

item.title: Hemingway Editor
item.description: Hemingway Editor takes its name from the writer known for short sentences. You paste or write text, and the app colors problems: long, dense sentences in yellow and red, adverbs in blue, passive voice in green, and simpler alternatives for complicated words in purple. A grade level score estimates how hard the writing is to read, and the aim is to bring it to a level most readers can follow easily.

item.title: HumanizerFree.com
item.description:
HumanizerFree takes text produced by an AI model and rewrites it with varied phrasing, sentence length, and word choices so it reads less like machine output. A user pastes text, runs the tool, and edits the result. The tool is free for basic use.

Such tools raise questions. Using them to hide AI use in contexts where it is prohibited, such as some schoolwork, may break rules and can count as academic dishonesty. AI detectors are unreliable, so humanizers do not guarantee any result, and a rewrite can introduce errors or awkward phrasing.

item.title: Humata
item.description: Humata lets people converse with documents. After you upload a file, it reads the content and answers questions about it: asking for a summary, a specific figure, a comparison between sections, or an explanation of a clause. Each answer includes a citation that links to the passage in the source, which makes it easy to verify. It works with long files that would take a long time to scan manually, such as contracts, research papers, and financial reports.

item.title: JetBrains AI Assistant
item.description: JetBrains AI Assistant works inside the IDEs that many professional developers already use. In IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, Rider, and the rest of the family, it provides inline completion, a chat panel that understands the project, and actions to explain code, generate tests, write commit messages, and suggest fixes for errors. Because it is built into the IDE, it can use the IDE’s deep knowledge of code structure, such as types, references, and run configurations.

item.title: Kin Personal AI
item.description:
Kin positions itself as a private personal AI. Users talk with an assistant that remembers their circumstances and offers guidance across areas of life, with specialized advisors that focus on different topics. The conversation builds a profile over time so advice reflects what the user has shared.

Privacy is the main selling point. The company states that personal data is stored locally on the device and encrypted, rather than in a central cloud, so sensitive details are less exposed. This appeals to people who want to discuss personal matters without handing data to a large platform.

item.title: Komos
item.description:
Komos aims to replace fragile recorded scripts with instructions in natural language. A user describes a task, such as downloading reports from a portal or entering data across systems, and an AI agent carries it out by operating a browser, adjusting when a page changes.

That approach targets a known weakness of traditional robotic process automation, where small interface changes break bots. Enterprise teams use such tools for back-office tasks in systems that lack APIs.

item.title: leania.ai
item.description:
Leania.ai analyzes how work flows through an organization. It ingests information such as organization charts, process documentation, and meeting data, and uses AI to identify where handoffs are slow, roles overlap, or responsibilities are unclear. It then suggests changes to improve efficiency.

The audience is operations and HR leaders planning restructuring or process improvement. Outputs aim to replace guesswork with data from the company’s own materials, though recommendations still require leaders to understand context and consult the people involved.

item.title: Littlebird
item.description:
Littlebird tries to understand what you are working on. It observes activity across apps, such as messages, meetings, documents, and web pages, and builds a memory of context. When a user asks for help, such as summarizing a project status or drafting a reply, it draws on that history.

The pitch is an assistant that does not need to be told everything each time. That convenience comes with a privacy tradeoff, since an always-on tool sees a lot of work content. Users should understand what is captured, where it is stored, and how to pause or delete it.

item.title: Logseq
item.description: Logseq is built on the idea that notes should be a network of connected blocks. You write in an outliner where each bullet is a block, link to other pages with double brackets, and see backlinks that show everywhere an idea is referenced. Daily journals are the default entry point, so you capture thoughts as they come and organize them through links instead of folders. A graph view shows how pages relate.

item.title: Lovable
item.description: Lovable lets people describe an app and get something that runs. You type what you want, such as a task tracker, a booking tool, or a customer portal, and it generates a React front end, sets up pages and components, and shows a live preview. You then keep chatting to change the layout, add features, or fix problems. It is popular with founders, designers, and product managers who want a prototype without a development team.

item.title: MagicSlides
item.description:
MagicSlides speeds up deck creation. A user enters a topic, pastes text, or uploads a document, and the tool builds slides with titles, bullets, and images. Because it works as an add-on inside Google Slides and PowerPoint, the results land in a familiar editor for refinement.

It supports many languages and offers themes and layouts. Students use it for assignments, and professionals use it to produce a first draft of a presentation, which they then edit. Images can be sourced automatically.

item.title: Mem
item.description:
Mem is built on the idea that notes should organize themselves. Users capture thoughts, meeting notes, and links without choosing folders, and the system connects related items and surfaces them when relevant. Search understands meaning, so finding an old idea does not require remembering exact words.

AI features extend this. A chat assistant answers questions using your notes, summarizes meetings, and drafts text from your own material. Integrations bring in content from calendars and other apps, so context accumulates in one place.

item.title: Mumble AI
item.description:
Mumble AI is built around talking instead of typing. Users dictate ideas or record meetings, and the app turns speech into structured notes, highlighting tasks and decisions. Apps on Mac and iPhone sync so a thought captured on the go is waiting at the desk.

It targets busy professionals who think out loud: managers between meetings, founders, and consultants. Features include summaries, task extraction, and searchable archives.

Independent information about Mumble AI is limited, so check where audio is processed and stored. It has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Otter, Granola, Superwhisper, Voicenotes, and Apple Notes with transcription. Mumble AI suits people who prefer to capture notes by voice.

item.title: NotebookLM
item.description: NotebookLM is built around the idea of grounding AI in your own sources. You create a notebook and add materials such as PDFs, Google Docs, web pages, YouTube videos, and pasted text. The AI answers questions using only those sources and shows citations that link to the exact passages, which reduces the risk of invented facts and makes answers easy to check. It is popular with students, researchers, writers, and professionals who work with a lot of reading.

item.title: Notion AI
item.description: Notion is a workspace for notes, documents, wikis, and databases, and Notion AI works inside it instead of in a separate chat window. Highlight a paragraph and ask it to tighten the writing, summarize a long page, translate a section, or turn rough notes into a clean doc. It can also fill in database properties, such as tagging each row with a category or pulling action items out of meeting notes, which saves a lot of manual cleanup in busy workspaces.

item.title: Notis
item.description:
Notis works where people already chat. Users send a text or voice note to the assistant in a messaging app, and it can save notes, draft emails, set tasks, search the web, or update tools like Notion and calendars. The aim is to reduce the friction of opening several apps.

Connections to services such as Gmail, Google Calendar, and Notion let the assistant act on requests, and it keeps a memory of preferences. Voice notes are transcribed and organized.

item.title: NovelAI
item.description: NovelAI started as a tool for writers who wanted an AI collaborator for fiction. In its editor, you write a passage and the AI continues it, with controls for style, memory, and the characters and world in your story. Features such as lorebooks store details about characters and places so the AI keeps them consistent, and you can edit, retry, and steer the output freely. It’s used by hobbyist novelists, roleplayers, and fan fiction writers.

item.title: Obsidian AI
item.description:
Obsidian’s approach to AI follows its general philosophy: keep the core simple and let users choose add-ons. Because notes are plain files in a folder, they work well with language models. Community plugins let you chat with your vault, ask questions about your notes, summarize long documents, rewrite text, and find related notes by meaning instead of keywords. Smart Connections and Copilot-style plugins are popular examples.

Users have a lot of freedom over where the AI runs. A plugin can send text to a hosted model like those from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google using your own API key, or it can connect to a local model through tools such as Ollama or LM Studio, so notes never leave your computer. Some people also expose their vault to coding agents and assistants through the Model Context Protocol, which lets tools like Claude read and organize notes.

item.title: Pipedream
item.description: Pipedream sits between no-code automation and writing everything yourself. You build workflows from triggers, such as a webhook or a new row in a sheet, and steps that either call a prebuilt action for an app or run your own code, with access to npm and PyPI packages. That mix lets developers move faster than in tools like Zapier while still handling logic that needs real programming, and it suits integrations and internal automations.

item.title: QuillBot
item.description:
QuillBot began as a paraphrasing tool and still draws most of its users for that. You paste in a passage, choose a mode such as standard, fluent, formal, or shorter, and it rewrites the text while keeping the meaning. A slider controls how much the wording changes. Students, non-native English speakers, and professional writers use it to rephrase awkward sentences, shorten drafts, and vary their style.

Around the paraphraser is a set of writing utilities. The grammar checker catches spelling and punctuation mistakes, the summarizer condenses long articles into key points or paragraphs, and the citation generator formats references in styles such as APA and MLA. A translator, an AI chat assistant, and detectors that estimate whether text is AI-written or plagiarized are included. Browser extensions and a Word add-in bring these tools into the places where people write.

item.title: Read AI
item.description:
Read AI began as a meeting analytics tool. It joins calls on Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and other platforms, then produces a transcript, summary, action items, and chapters. What set it apart was measurement: reports on engagement, speaker time, and sentiment, giving meeting organizers a sense of how a conversation went and who participated.

The product has expanded across communication channels. Read AI can summarize emails and messages, and its search and Q&A features answer questions across meetings, email, and chat, so you can ask what was decided about a project or what a client said last month. Integrations send summaries to Slack, Notion, Salesforce, and HubSpot. A copilot can prepare you for upcoming meetings by pulling relevant history.

item.title: Recall
item.description:
Recall acts as a personal archive that organizes itself. A user saves a web page, YouTube video, podcast, or document with a browser extension or app, and Recall produces a summary, extracts key points, and links the item to related content already in the library through a knowledge graph.

An assistant lets users ask questions across everything they have saved, and spaced repetition quizzes help them remember material. It suits people who consume a lot of information and lose track of it.

item.title: Reclaim AI
item.description:
Reclaim is a smart scheduling assistant. You tell it your priorities, tasks with deadlines, recurring habits such as lunch or exercise, and preferred meeting hours, and it places them in your calendar. When a new meeting appears, Reclaim moves flexible items around automatically, so your calendar stays workable without constant manual rescheduling.

Several features support teams. Smart one-on-ones find times that work for both participants and adjust over time, scheduling links let others book you at times that fit your priorities, and focus time blocks protect deep work. Integrations pull tasks from tools like Asana, ClickUp, Todoist, Linear, and Jira and schedule them, and analytics show how you spend time.

item.title: Reflect
item.description:
Reflect aims to be a quick place to capture thoughts and connect them. You write notes, link them to each other with simple syntax, and see backlinks that show where an idea is referenced. Daily notes serve as an inbox, a calendar view ties notes to meetings, and a graph helps visualize connections. The app is built for speed and a clean interface, with sync across devices.

The AI assistant works on your notes. It can summarize a page, rewrite text, brainstorm, and answer questions based on the content you have saved, and voice transcription turns spoken notes into text. Reflect also emphasizes privacy: notes are end-to-end encrypted, which limits what the company can see. Browser extensions and integrations let you save web content and connect with services like Kindle highlights and Readwise.

item.title: remio
item.description:
remio collects what you read and write in one place and lets you ask questions about it. It indexes notes, files, and web pages visited, then answers queries such as where an idea came from or what a document said, with links to the source.

The idea is to address the problem of forgetting where information lives. Capture happens automatically through a browser extension and app, with less manual filing than a traditional note tool.

item.title: Rocket
item.description:
Rocket belongs to the prompt-to-app builders. A user describes the product, and the platform generates the interface, back end logic, and database, previews it, and deploys it. Further changes are made through conversation, with the option to edit code.

It targets founders and operators who want to test an idea or build an internal tool without engineers. As with similar tools, generated apps need testing, and security and data handling deserve review before real users arrive.

item.title: Rytr
item.description:
Rytr is a simple, affordable writing assistant. You pick a use case, such as a blog section, an ad, a job description, or an email, choose a tone, and give a short brief, and it generates a draft in seconds. It supports many languages and has built-in rewriting and expansion tools, plus a plagiarism checker in higher plans.

The editor resembles a text document, so you can generate content and edit it in one place. Rytr is used by freelancers, small businesses, and students who want quick drafts without learning complex tools, and its price is lower than many competitors. Chrome extensions and an API help use it elsewhere.

item.title: Serno
item.description:
Serno gives users a single place to consult multiple models. A person asks a question once and sees how different systems respond, with differences highlighted, which can reveal uncertainty or disagreement that a single answer would hide.

This approach suits research, strategy, and decisions where one model’s blind spot could mislead. Saved conversations and comparisons make it easy to revisit reasoning, and some workflows ask models to critique each other.

item.title: Slack AI
item.description:
Slack AI addresses the problem of catching up. When you return from time off or join a busy channel, it can summarize what happened, list decisions, and highlight what needs your attention. Thread summaries cut long discussions into a few lines, and daily recaps cover channels you choose, so you can stay informed without reading every message.

AI search turns Slack into a place to ask questions. Instead of hunting for keywords, you can ask something like what the timeline is for a project, and receive an answer drawn from messages, files, and connected apps, with links to the sources. Slackbot is being reshaped as an assistant that can help draft messages, find information, and take actions, and Salesforce’s Agentforce agents can work in Slack. Huddle notes summarize audio calls.

item.title: Slashspace
item.description:
Slashspace rethinks chatting with AI as a workspace instead of a single scrolling thread. Conversations live on a canvas where users branch ideas, keep multiple threads open, and combine sources, so research does not get buried in a long chat history.

The app supports several models, lets users bring in documents and web pages, and keeps context organized. Writers and analysts use it to explore a topic from different angles and compare lines of reasoning.

item.title: Sudowrite
item.description:
Sudowrite is designed for fiction writers. Instead of a generic chatbot, it provides tools shaped around storytelling: a Describe function that expands a moment with sensory detail, Rewrite options that change tone or style, Brainstorm tools for names, plot twists, and settings, and a feature to continue a scene in your voice. Writers can paste their own text and have the AI follow its style.

The platform has bigger story-level tools as well. Story Engine helps build a novel from a premise by generating characters, outlines, and chapters that the writer edits, and it keeps a database of story details so the AI maintains consistency. Sudowrite developed its own model focused on prose, and offers features for feedback and revision. It has appealed to authors who want a collaborator for drafting.

item.title: Team Pulse
item.description:
Team Pulse offers tasks, boards, and status views for small teams. AI helps summarize progress, flag risks, and keep everyone informed, aiming to reduce the status meetings and check-ins that eat time.

The product competes with well-known tools and aims at teams that find larger platforms heavy. Common features include assignments, deadlines, and dashboards that show workload.

Independent information is limited, so evaluate it with a trial, including integrations and export options. It has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Asana, Monday.com, ClickUp, Linear, and Trello. Team Pulse suits small teams looking for a simple tracker.

item.title: TheLibrarian.io
item.description:
TheLibrarian.io puts an assistant in WhatsApp. Users message it to check their email, schedule events, create tasks, and get reminders, in natural language or voice notes. It connects to services like Gmail and Google Calendar.

The appeal is simplicity: no new interface, and the chat is available anywhere. Connecting an assistant to email and calendars requires trust, so review permissions and privacy terms.

Independent information is limited. It has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Notis, Poke, Lindy, Motion, and ChatGPT with connectors. TheLibrarian.io suits people who want to manage tasks through WhatsApp.

item.title: v0 by Vercel
item.description: v0 started as a tool for generating user interface components from text. You described a pricing table or dashboard, and it produced React code styled with Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui components that you could copy into a project. It has since grown into a full app builder: you can ask for pages, forms, and logic, upload a wireframe or screenshot to recreate, and watch a live preview update as you refine the result in conversation.

item.title: Windsurf
item.description: Windsurf was built by the Codeium team as an editor designed around AI from the start, in contrast to adding assistants to an existing IDE. Its Cascade agent understands the project, edits multiple files, runs terminal commands, and reasons about changes while you watch. A fast Tab completion feature predicts what you will write next, and previews let you see a running web app inside the editor and ask for changes visually. It started from VS Code, so extensions and settings carry over.

item.title: Wispr Flow
item.description:
Wispr Flow turns speech into polished text. A user presses a key, talks, and the cleaned-up text appears wherever the cursor is. The AI removes filler words, fixes false starts, handles punctuation, and adjusts tone to the app, so messages and documents read as if typed.

It supports many languages, custom vocabulary for names and terms, and commands for editing by voice. Writers, developers, and professionals use it to speed up emails, notes, and prompts for AI tools.

item.title: Wordtune
item.description: Wordtune is built around rewriting. Highlight a sentence in your draft and it offers several alternatives: shorter, longer, more casual, or more formal. You pick the one that sounds right and keep your own voice instead of pasting in a block of generated text. That makes it more of an editor’s tool than a text generator, which suits people who already know what they want to say and need help phrasing it.

item.title: WriteABookAI
item.description:
WriteABookAI helps authors move from idea to manuscript. A writer enters a premise, and the tool proposes an outline, character profiles, and chapter drafts, which can be edited. It aims at fiction and nonfiction, with tools to track plot and consistency.

Fully AI-drafted books tend to be generic and may contain errors or contradictions, and publishing platforms and readers expect disclosure of AI use. The best outcomes come from writers who use the tool as a drafting aid and add their own voice and expertise.

item.title: ZeroTwo
item.description:
ZeroTwo is a multi-model chat workspace. A user picks a model for each conversation or compares several, and keeps history, files, and prompts in one place. It supports web search, image generation, and document analysis.

For people who use several AI products, a combined interface can simplify life and cost. Pricing is typically a single subscription instead of many.

Access to the newest features of each provider may lag the official apps. ZeroTwo has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Poe, TypingMind, ChatHub, OpenRouter’s chat, and Open WebUI. ZeroTwo suits power users who work across models.

item.title: Zoom AI Companion
item.description: AI Companion is the assistant built into Zoom’s meeting, chat, phone, and document tools. Its most used feature is the meeting summary: it listens to the call, produces a transcript, and writes up the main points and action items, which it can share with attendees right after the meeting ends. If you join late, it can catch you up on what was said. It can also answer questions about a meeting in progress, such as what was decided on a topic a few minutes ago.
